title: What hosting actually is
description: Your project running on your own laptop and your project being reachable by anyone, anywhere, are two completely different things — hosting is what closes that gap, and it means paying someone to keep a computer on, connected, and reachable.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the difference between a project running locally and a project that's actually hosted
Identify what a hosting provider is actually selling, and what happens past its free tier

contentSections.title: It works on your laptop. That's not the same as working.

contentSections.body: You've been building a project for weeks. It runs perfectly — `npm run dev`, open `localhost:3000`, there it is. You text a friend: "check out what I built, [link]" and then realize there is no link. localhost:3000 means "this computer, port 3000" — on your friend's phone, that address points at their own phone, which isn't running anything. Nothing you've built so far has ever left your machine.

contentSections.scenario: Four things that are all, in some loose sense, "on a computer": (1) a React app running via localhost:3000 on your laptop, (2) that same app pushed to a private GitHub repository, (3) that same app running on a server that's always on, has a public IP address, and is configured to accept incoming requests, (4) a Google Doc you've shared with view access.
contentSections.question: Which of these is actually reachable by a stranger typing an address into their own browser, right now?

options.label: Only (3) — a server that's on, publicly addressable, and accepting requests
(2) and (3) — anything that's been uploaded somewhere counts as hosted
All four — they're all "on the internet" in some sense

feedback.server: Right. GitHub storing your code (2) is not the same as anyone being able to run it — a private repo is a backup, not a website. What makes (3) different is specific: a machine that stays on, has a public address, and is actively listening for requests and answering them. That combination is what "hosted" actually means.
feedback.uploaded: Uploading code somewhere (GitHub) is storage, not hosting — nothing about a repository makes the code *run* for a visitor, and a private repo isn't even reachable without permission. The distinguishing feature of (3) is that it's a running, addressable, publicly reachable process, not a stored file.
feedback.all: A Google Doc being viewable and a codebase being *runnable* by a stranger are different categories of thing entirely — a shared doc's server is Google's, already running, already addressed. Your own project has none of that until something equivalent is set up for it specifically.

contentSections.concept: Hosting means three things happening at once, for one specific piece of software you wrote: a computer that is switched on right now, that has a public address the rest of the internet can find, and that is actively running your code and answering requests for it. Your laptop can do all three, technically — the problem is it isn't doing them reliably, it isn't on all the time, and most home internet connections don't give you a stable public address anyway.

contentSections.body: A hosting provider's actual product is unglamorous: a computer, kept on, connected, and configured to run your code and answer requests — for as long as you keep paying, or as long as you stay inside a free tier's limits. Vercel, Netlify, Render, Railway and a hundred others are all selling variations of the same three things: compute (a machine running your code), bandwidth (data flowing to visitors), and uptime (the promise that machine stays on). The free tiers most beginners start on are real and genuinely usable for a small project — Vercel's free tier, for instance, includes 100GB of bandwidth a month and generous build minutes as of this writing. What it doesn't include: commercial use past certain limits, and if traffic spikes past the free allowance, the free tier response is typically to throttle or pause the site, not silently bill you — but that varies by provider and is worth reading before you rely on it for anything real.

The other half of "hosted" is the address itself. Every hosted project gets a free subdomain from its provider on deploy — something like `your-project-a1b2.vercel.app` — which is a completely real, working, shareable URL from the moment your first deploy finishes. A custom domain (`yourproject.com`) is a separate purchase, layered on top later; lesson five covers what that actually costs. Nothing about getting a project onto the internet requires owning a domain name first.

contentSections.scenario: A learner says: "I ran `npm run build` and it says 'build successful' — but when I email the folder to my friend, they can't get it to work at all, and there's no link to share."
contentSections.question: What's actually missing here?

options.label: A build succeeding produces files on disk — it doesn't put anything on a server anyone else can reach
The build must have actually failed, despite the success message
The friend needs to also run npm run build on their own computer first

feedback.no-server: Right. `npm run build` produces a folder of static files — HTML, CSS, JS — sitting on the local disk. That's real and necessary, but it's still just files on one computer. Nothing has made those files reachable from anywhere else; that's a separate step (deploying) covered in the next lesson, and it's the step that was skipped here.
feedback.build-failed: The message says success, and there's no reason to doubt it — a successful build genuinely does produce working output files. The problem isn't that the build lied; it's that a successful build and a *hosted* site are two different, separate accomplishments.
feedback.friend-build: Emailing a folder of built files and asking someone to run them locally sort of works for a technical friend with the right tools installed, but it isn't hosting, it isn't a shareable link, and it completely breaks down for literally anyone else who wants to see the project.

contentSections.mechanism: A build step and a deploy step solve two different problems. Building takes your source code and produces the actual files a browser needs (this is lesson three's whole subject). Deploying takes those files and puts them on a server that's on, addressable, and listening — which is the only thing that turns "I have files that would work if you had a server" into "here's a link." Skipping straight from build success to "why can't my friend see it" is skipping the entire second step.

contentSections.body: Hosting is a computer that's on, publicly addressable, and running your code — your laptop can theoretically do all three, but a hosting provider does them reliably, which is the entire thing you're paying for (or getting free, within limits).

contentSections.title: What actually breaks past the free tier

contentSections.body: A free hosting tier feels like a solved problem until it isn't: a project that was fine for months suddenly returns errors, or stops deploying, because a specific number was crossed — a bandwidth cap, a build-minutes allowance, a function-invocation limit — and nobody was watching for it.

contentSections.scenario: A small personal project — a portfolio site, a handful of visitors a day — is hosted on a typical free tier that includes 100GB of bandwidth per month. Bandwidth is roughly the total size of everything downloaded by everyone who visits, added up across the month.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many page visits, at an average of 2MB per visit (images included), would it take to use up that entire 100GB monthly allowance?
contentSections.explanation: 100GB ÷ 2MB per visit is 50,000 visits. For a small personal project getting a few dozen visits a day, that's essentially unreachable — which is exactly why free tiers are genuinely fine for learning projects and small real ones. The number to actually worry about isn't the free allowance itself; it's whether a specific page (an unoptimized image, an accidentally-public API route that gets hit in a loop) is unusually heavy, since a handful of very large downloads matter more than a lot of small ones.

contentSections.body: The free-tier failure that actually catches people isn't heavy human traffic — it's usually one of: an unoptimized asset (a 40MB video embedded directly instead of linked from somewhere built for video), a bug that causes a page to be requested in a loop, or a limit that has nothing to do with bandwidth at all, like a cap on serverless function invocations or build minutes per month. Reading the specific free tier's limits once, at the start, is a five-minute task that prevents a very confusing afternoon later — and every major provider publishes them plainly rather than hiding them, because a surprised free-tier user is a bad look for the provider too.
A hosting provider's free tier is a computer, an address, and a promise of uptime, given away up to a specific, published limit — knowing that limit before you need it is five minutes well spent.

title: Deploying a static site, start to finish
description: The actual sequence, once, in full: code in a GitHub repo, connected to a host, deployed automatically on every push — the same four steps regardless of which specific host you pick.

learningObjectives.text: Deploy a static site from a GitHub repository to a hosting provider

contentSections.title: The same four steps, every time

contentSections.body: A static site — plain HTML/CSS/JS, or the built output of a framework, with no server-side code running per request — is the simplest thing to deploy, and walking through it once, completely, is what makes every later, more complicated deploy make sense.

contentSections.problem: Deploy a static portfolio site (index.html, styles.css, a couple of images) so it has a real, public URL.

steps.label: Push the code to GitHub
steps.work: git init, git add ., git commit -m "initial site", create a repo on GitHub, git push.
steps.why: Every major host deploys from a Git repository, not from files uploaded by hand — this is what makes step 4 (deploy on every push) possible at all.

steps.label: Create an account with a host and connect the repo
steps.work: Sign up at a provider (Vercel, Netlify, and similar all work the same way for this), authorize it to access your GitHub account, and pick the specific repository.
steps.why: The host needs permission to read your repo so it can pull the code and build/serve it — this is a one-time authorization, not something repeated per deploy.

steps.label: Confirm the settings and deploy
steps.work: For a plain static site there's usually nothing to configure — the host detects there's no build step needed and serves the files as they are. Click deploy.
steps.why: A framework project needs a build command and output directory specified here (lesson three); a plain static site skips straight to serving the files that already exist.

steps.label: Get the URL, and push again to update it
steps.work: The host gives you a working URL immediately (`your-site-a1b2.netlify.app`). Change something locally, commit, and push — the site updates automatically within a minute or two, with no extra steps.
steps.why: This is the actual payoff of connecting to Git instead of uploading files by hand: every push becomes a deploy, automatically, forever, without repeating any of the earlier steps.

faded.problem: Deploy a different static project — a single-page HTML resume with one CSS file — using the same host.

blanks.prompt: Before connecting a host at all, what has to exist first?
blanks.answer: The code pushed to a GitHub repository
accept: Code committed and pushed to GitHub
blanks.why: Every host in this workflow deploys from a Git repository — without that, there is nothing for the host to connect to.

blanks.prompt: After the host is connected and the first deploy finishes, what do you have?
blanks.answer: A real, working URL on the host's own subdomain
blanks.why: The free subdomain is live from the very first successful deploy, with no custom domain required.

blanks.prompt: You fix a typo in the HTML locally. What's the entire process to get that fix live?
blanks.answer: Commit and push the change to GitHub
blanks.why: This is the whole point of connecting to Git in the first place — once connected, every push redeploys automatically with no manual steps.

contentSections.procedure: Push to GitHub, connect a host to that repository, confirm the (often empty, for plain static files) build settings and deploy once, then every future push redeploys automatically.

contentSections.question: Put these into the actual order they happen in, deploying a static site for the first time:
steps: Push the project to a GitHub repository
Create a hosting account and authorize it to access GitHub
Connect the specific repository and confirm the deploy settings
Get a live URL from the first successful deploy
Push a later change and watch it redeploy automatically
contentSections.explanation: The one step people try to skip is the first — connecting a host directly to a folder on your computer, instead of to a GitHub repo. Some hosts technically allow a manual drag-and-drop upload for a one-off deploy, but it breaks the entire automatic-redeploy-on-push workflow, which is the actual value of this setup. Once it's wired to GitHub, every future update is a `git push` and nothing else.

contentSections.body: Deploying a static site is four steps, done once: push to GitHub, connect a host, confirm settings, deploy — and after that, every push is the whole update process.

title: Build steps and what happens to your code on the way
description: The code you write and the code that actually ships are usually not the same files — a build step transforms, bundles and minifies your source into what a browser actually receives, and telling a host the wrong output directory is the single most common reason a deploy "succeeds" and still shows a blank page.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a build step does to source code before it's deployed
Diagnose a deploy that succeeds but serves a blank page as an output-directory misconfiguration

contentSections.title: Your source code is not what the browser receives

contentSections.body: A React project's source lives in a `src/` folder full of `.jsx` files, imports, and JavaScript a browser can't actually run directly. Running `npm run build` doesn't just copy those files somewhere — it produces a completely different folder (commonly `dist/` or `build/`), full of plain `.html`, `.js` and `.css` files, often with unfamiliar names, that a browser can actually run.

contentSections.scenario: A build step for a typical React project does several things at once: converts JSX syntax into plain JavaScript function calls a browser understands, combines dozens of separate imported files into a small number of bundled files, removes comments and shortens variable names (minification) to cut file size, and sometimes converts newer JavaScript syntax into an older, more widely-supported form.
contentSections.question: Given all of that, is the code that actually ends up running in a visitor's browser the same code you wrote?

options.label: No — it's a transformed, bundled, minified version, functionally equivalent but not the same text
Yes, exactly — a build step just copies the files as-is to a new location
No — the build step rewrites the actual logic, not just the syntax

feedback.transformed: Right. A build step is a real transformation, not a copy: JSX becomes plain function calls, many files become few, whitespace and comments disappear, variable names get shortened. What it deliberately does not do is change what the code *does* — the behavior is preserved even though the actual text is unrecognizable, which is exactly why you can open a deployed site's dev tools and see strange, minified code that still works correctly.
feedback.same: A build step does considerably more than copying — open a built file in `dist/` next to its source in `src/` and they look nothing alike. Minification alone renames variables and strips whitespace; bundling combines many files into few.
feedback.logic-changed: The transformation preserves behavior deliberately — a build tool's entire job is to produce code that does exactly what the source does, just in a form a browser can run and that's smaller and faster to download. If the logic changed, that would be a bug in the build tool, not its intended function.

contentSections.concept: A build step turns human-authored source code into what a browser can actually and efficiently run: transforming syntax the browser doesn't understand, bundling many files into few, and minifying to cut download size — all while preserving exactly what the code does. This is why deploying "the project" almost always means deploying the *build output*, not the source files you actually wrote.

contentSections.body: This is also exactly why a hosting provider needs to be told two things for anything beyond a plain static site: the **build command** (what to run — typically `npm run build`) and the **output directory** (where the result lands — commonly `dist`, `build`, or `out`, depending on the tool). Get the output directory wrong — point the host at `src` instead of `dist`, or a `dist` from an old, stale build — and the deploy will often report success (the build command ran without an error) while serving something wrong: blank, outdated, or a raw folder listing instead of a working site.

contentSections.scenario: A deploy log shows: `Build completed successfully. Deploying...`. The URL loads, but the page is completely blank — no error in the browser console, just an empty white page.
contentSections.question: Given the build genuinely succeeded, what's the most likely cause of a blank deployed page?

options.label: The host is configured to serve the wrong output directory — an empty or stale folder, not the one the build just produced
The build must have secretly failed despite the success message
Blank pages after a successful build are always a browser caching problem

feedback.wrong-dir: Right. A build succeeding and the host serving the correct output are two separate facts — the build log confirms the first, not the second. A misconfigured output directory (pointing at `build` when the tool actually outputs to `dist`, for example) means the host is serving an empty or unrelated folder, and there's nothing in the build log itself that would catch that mismatch.
feedback.secret-fail: The log's success message is genuinely reliable for what it reports — the build process ran to completion without an error. What it can't tell you is whether the *next* step (serving the right folder) is configured correctly, because that's a separate setting entirely.
feedback.cache: A caching issue is worth ruling out with a hard refresh, but it wouldn't typically start with a totally blank page on a fresh visit from a device that's never loaded the site before — a genuinely wrong output directory produces exactly this symptom reliably.

contentSections.mechanism: Every host has a specific setting for "which folder, after the build finishes, actually gets served to visitors." That setting is independent of whether the build command itself succeeded — a build can complete cleanly and still leave the host pointed at the wrong place, an old stale folder, or nowhere real at all. The fix is always the same: check what folder the build tool actually outputs to (read its docs, or look at what appeared locally after running the build command), and make sure the host's output-directory setting matches it exactly.

contentSections.body: A build succeeding and a build being served correctly are two separate facts — a blank page after a clean build is almost always the host pointed at the wrong output folder, not a broken build.

contentSections.title: Committing build output is a trap, not a shortcut

contentSections.body: A tempting shortcut: commit the `dist` folder itself to the repository, so there's no build step to configure at all — just serve what's already there. It works, once, and then quietly rots.

contentSections.code:
# .gitignore
node_modules/

# but dist/ is committed to the repo directly,
# and the host is set to just serve dist/ with no build command
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with committing dist/ and skipping the build step on the host entirely?

options.label: Every future deploy now depends on someone remembering to rebuild locally and commit the new dist/ — one missed rebuild ships stale code with no error anywhere
Git can't store built files at all, so this would fail immediately
Nothing is actually wrong with this — it removes a step, which is strictly simpler

feedback.stale: Right. This trades a small one-time setup cost (configuring the build command once, correctly) for a permanent, invisible manual step forever after: a source change with no matching rebuild-and-recommit produces a repo where the source and the deployed dist/ have quietly diverged, and there is no error message anywhere to catch it — the site just keeps serving old behavior.
feedback.cant-store: Git stores any files handed to it, built output included — this would work mechanically without any error. The problem isn't technical failure, it's the process trap it creates.
feedback.fine: It looks simpler for exactly one deploy. The cost shows up on the second one: a change to source with no matching manual rebuild leaves the deployed dist/ silently out of date, and nothing will flag that mismatch — it just becomes a bug that looks unrelated to the actual cause.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Letting the host run the build command itself (rather than committing pre-built output) means the deployed site is always built from whatever's actually in the source right now — there's no separate, human-maintained copy that can drift out of sync. It costs one extra field to configure the first time, and removes an entire category of "why is the live site still showing the old version" bug forever after.

contentSections.body: The practical rule: `dist/`, `build/`, and any other generated output folder belongs in `.gitignore`, not in the repository, and the host's build command is what regenerates it fresh on every single deploy. This also means a fresh clone of the repo — on a new laptop, or a teammate's machine — never has stale built files lying around to confuse anyone; running the build command is always the single source of truth for what actually ships.
Committing build output as a shortcut trades a one-time setup cost for a permanent, invisible manual step — letting the host rebuild from source on every deploy is what actually removes the risk.

title: Environment variables and secrets in production
description: A key committed to a public repository is compromised permanently, the instant it's pushed, even if it's deleted in the very next commit — environment variables set in a host's dashboard, never written into the code itself, are what keep production secrets actually secret.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a specific way of handling a secret in production is actually safe

contentSections.title: Deleting a secret from the code doesn't delete it from history

contentSections.body: A developer hardcodes an API key directly into a file, commits it, realizes the mistake an hour later, deletes the line, and commits again with the message "remove exposed key." The key is still fully exposed — anyone can look at the repository's commit history, find the earlier commit, and read it out, forever, unless the key itself is revoked at the source.

contentSections.question: This file (with real keys in place of these placeholders) gets pushed to a public repository, then the keys are deleted in the very next commit. What's actually still true?

options.label: The original keys are permanently recoverable from the repo's commit history, regardless of what the latest commit shows
Deleting the line in the next commit fully removes the exposure
It's only a real problem if the repo stays public — a private repo would be completely safe with this pattern

feedback.still-exposed: Right. Git history is exactly that — history. Every previous commit remains fully accessible (`git log`, browsing old commits on GitHub, a clone made before the deletion) unless the entire history is rewritten and force-pushed, which is disruptive and easy to get wrong. The only response that actually neutralizes an exposed key is revoking it at the provider (Stripe, Anthropic, wherever it came from) and issuing a new one — the same act as changing a lock rather than hoping nobody used the old key.
feedback.fixed: The deletion only affects what the *current* version of the file shows — every commit before it, containing the real key in plain text, is still there and still readable by anyone with access to the repository's history.
feedback.private-safe: A private repo genuinely reduces who can see it, and matters — but "safe" is the wrong word once real credentials are hardcoded anywhere in a project: every collaborator, every CI log that might print the file, and anyone who gains access later (a leaked personal access token, a repo that's later made public by accident) can read it. The actual fix is not putting the secret in the code at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The failure here isn't the typo or the specific key — it's putting any real secret directly into source code at all, which makes it permanently part of the project's history the moment it's committed. Environment variables, set through the hosting provider's dashboard and never written into a file that gets committed, are what avoid this category of mistake entirely — the actual secret never becomes text that Git tracks.

contentSections.body: An environment variable is a value set outside the code — in a `.env` file locally (which belongs in `.gitignore`, never committed) and in the hosting provider's dashboard for production. The code references it by name only — something like `process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` — and never contains the actual value anywhere that gets committed. This is the entire mechanism: the real secret exists in exactly two places, your local `.env` file and the host's environment-variable settings, both of which are outside the Git history.

A secret hardcoded into a file is exposed permanently the moment it's committed, deletion in a later commit included — environment variables, set outside the codebase entirely, are what keep it out of history in the first place.

contentSections.title: Setting it in the dashboard, and what changes between local and production

contentSections.body: Locally, `.env` is a plain text file with lines like `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=<value>`, read automatically by most frameworks and never committed. In production, there's no `.env` file at all on the server — the equivalent step is typing the same name and value into the hosting provider's dashboard, under a section usually called Environment Variables.

contentSections.scenario: A project needs a Stripe secret key available in production. Several proposed approaches are on the table.
contentSections.question: Select every approach that actually keeps the key out of the Git repository's history.

items.label: Set it as an environment variable in the hosting provider's dashboard
Keep it in a local .env file that's listed in .gitignore, and set the same variable separately in the dashboard for production
Hardcode it in config.js, then add config.js to .gitignore after the fact
Put it in a code comment instead of an active line, so it's 'just documentation'

explanation.dashboard: Keeps it out of history entirely. The value never exists as text in any file Git tracks — it lives only in the provider's own systems and is injected into the running process at deploy time.
explanation.gitignored-env: This is the standard, correct pattern: local development reads from a `.env` file Git never sees, and production reads the same variable name from the dashboard. Neither location ever becomes a commit.
explanation.hardcode-then-gitignore: Adding a file to `.gitignore` only stops *future* commits from tracking changes to it — if the file with the real key was already committed even once before the `.gitignore` entry was added, that commit and the key inside it are still sitting in history, fully readable.
explanation.comment: A commented-out line is still plain text in the committed file, fully visible to anyone who reads the source or its history — commenting something out changes whether it *runs*, not whether it's *exposed*.

contentSections.synthesis: The one property that actually matters is whether the real value ever becomes text inside a file that gets committed to Git, even once, even briefly. Everything that avoids that — environment variables locally and in the host's dashboard — is safe. Everything that puts the real value in a tracked file, even temporarily or in a comment, is exposed the moment it's pushed, and staying exposed is the default until the credential itself is revoked at the source.

contentSections.body: The only property that matters is whether a real secret ever becomes committed text — environment variables, local and in the host's dashboard, are how you make sure it never does.

title: A custom domain, and what it costs
description: A custom domain is a yearly rental, not a purchase — a specific, ongoing cost, on top of hosting, that lapses and can be lost entirely if a renewal is missed.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a custom domain actually costs on an ongoing basis
Connect a purchased domain to a hosted project via DNS records

contentSections.title: You're renting a name, every year, forever

contentSections.body: A domain name feels like something you buy once, the way you'd buy a book. What actually happens at checkout on a registrar like Namecheap or Porkbun is a one-year rental — the price shown is per year, and if that yearly renewal is ever missed, the domain becomes available for anyone else to register, including someone specifically watching for expired domains with existing traffic or backlinks.

contentSections.scenario: A common .com domain, registered through a typical registrar, with no premium or auction pricing involved.
contentSections.question: Roughly what does a standard .com domain cost per year, in USD, as of the current market?
contentSections.explanation: Most standard .com domains run somewhere around $10-15/year at a typical registrar, though the exact number moves with the market and some registrars run a cheap first-year promotional price that jumps at renewal — worth checking the renewal price specifically, not just the price shown at checkout. Other extensions vary a lot: some are cheaper, some (like many single-word .ai or .io domains) considerably more, and a handful of extensions are effectively unaffordable auction items. This is separate from hosting cost entirely — a domain is a name, hosting is compute — and most projects need both if they want a custom address instead of the free provider subdomain.

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely different cost from hosting, and easy to conflate: hosting can be free or cheap and pays for compute and bandwidth; a domain is a small, separate, recurring rental for a specific name, paid to a registrar (Namecheap, Porkbun, Google Domains and others), unrelated to which host actually runs your code. A project can use a free host with a custom domain, a paid host with the free subdomain, or any other combination — the two purchases are independent.
A domain is a yearly rental with a real, ongoing cost — separate from hosting entirely, and one that lapses (and can be permanently lost) if a renewal is ever missed.

contentSections.title: Pointing a name at a project: what DNS records actually do

contentSections.body: Buying `yourproject.com` doesn't automatically connect it to anything — a registrar sells names, not hosting. Making that name actually point at the deployed project is a separate step: adding DNS records that most hosts walk you through directly.

contentSections.problem: Connect a purchased domain, `yourproject.com`, to a project already deployed and live at `your-project-a1b2.vercel.app`.

steps.label: Add the domain in the host's dashboard
steps.work: In the hosting provider's project settings, add "yourproject.com" as a custom domain.
steps.why: This tells the host to expect and accept requests for that domain, and it's typically where the host tells you exactly which DNS records to add next.

steps.label: Go to the domain registrar's DNS settings
steps.work: Log into the registrar where the domain was purchased (not the host) and find its DNS management page.
steps.why: DNS records live with whoever manages the domain's DNS — usually the registrar by default, though it's sometimes delegated elsewhere. This is a different login and a different company from the host.

steps.label: Add the records the host specified
steps.work: Typically an A record (pointing the bare domain at an IP address) and/or a CNAME record (pointing a subdomain like www at the host's own address) — the host's dashboard gives the exact values to enter.
steps.why: These records are what actually tell the rest of the internet's DNS system where to send a browser that types in yourproject.com — without them, the domain resolves to nothing, regardless of how the host is configured.

steps.label: Wait for DNS to propagate, then verify
steps.work: Changes can take anywhere from minutes to (rarely) up to 48 hours to spread across the internet's DNS servers. The host's dashboard usually shows a checkmark once it detects the records are live.
steps.why: DNS propagation delay is normal and not a sign anything is broken — it's the reason 'I just added the records and it's not working yet' five minutes later is usually just a timing issue, not a misconfiguration.

faded.problem: Connect a different domain, `mynewapp.io`, purchased at a different registrar, to a project hosted on Netlify.

blanks.prompt: Where do you start — the registrar or the host?
blanks.answer: The host, adding the domain in its dashboard first
blanks.why: The host is what tells you exactly which records to add, so starting there gives you the specific values you need before touching the registrar.

blanks.prompt: Where do the actual DNS records get added?
blanks.answer: At the domain registrar's DNS settings, not the host
blanks.why: The host doesn't control the domain's DNS unless it was also bought there — DNS records live wherever the domain's DNS is managed, which by default is the registrar.

blanks.prompt: After adding the records, why might it not work immediately?
blanks.answer: DNS propagation delay — it can take minutes to hours to spread
blanks.why: This is a normal, expected delay, not a sign the records were entered wrong.

contentSections.procedure: Add the domain in the host's dashboard to get the exact records needed, add those records at the registrar where the domain's DNS is managed, then wait for propagation and verify.

contentSections.body: A domain and a host are two separate purchases from two separate companies — connecting them means adding DNS records, at the registrar, pointing the name at the host, and then waiting out normal propagation delay.

title: Practice — Diagnose Seven Failed Deployments
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a deploy that's broken in a specific way, diagnose the actual cause using this module's ideas — hosting, build output, environment variables, and DNS.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a specific failed deployment using the module's core distinctions

contentSections.title: Seven broken deploys, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: what hosting actually requires, what a build step produces and where it needs to be pointed, keeping secrets out of committed code, and how a custom domain actually connects to a host.
The same real question every time: what specifically is different between what's configured and what the project actually needs?

title: Lab — Deploy Your Project to a Real URL
description: Take a real project of yours and put it on the internet at a real, working address — with the build reproducible from a completely fresh clone, not just working on your own already-configured machine.

learningObjectives.text: Deploy a real project to a public URL using a Git-connected host
Verify a deployed project's build is reproducible from a fresh clone, not dependent on local machine state

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Take a real project from earlier in this track — even a small one is enough. By the end of this lab it has a live URL anyone can visit, and you'll have personally proven the build works from nothing, not just on the machine that's had months of installs and configuration accumulate on it.

contentSections.title: Deploy your project to a real URL
contentSections.brief: Pick a real project — ideally one you've already built earlier in this track. Prepare it properly, connect it to a host, deploy it, and then prove the whole thing is reproducible by cloning it fresh somewhere else and confirming it still builds and runs identically.
contentSections.deliverable: A live URL anyone can visit, with the build reproducible from a fresh clone.

stages.title: Prepare the project for deployment
stages.instructions: Confirm the build command actually works locally (`npm run build` or equivalent, with no errors). Check .gitignore covers node_modules/, any build output folder, and .env — and that no real secret is committed anywhere in the project's history. Make sure the repo is pushed to GitHub.
stages.checkpoint: The build runs cleanly locally, .gitignore is correct, and a search of the repo turns up no committed secrets.

stages.title: Connect a host and deploy
stages.instructions: Create an account with a host (Vercel, Netlify, Render, or similar), connect the GitHub repository, configure the build command and output directory if the project needs one, and set any required environment variables directly in the host's dashboard — never in a committed file.
stages.checkpoint: The first deploy succeeds and produces a real, working URL you can open in a browser.

stages.title: Verify from a completely fresh clone
stages.instructions: In a different folder (or, better, ask someone else, or use a throwaway cloud environment), clone the repository fresh and run the exact build command with no other setup. If it doesn't work identically to what's deployed, something is depending on local machine state that isn't actually in the repo — find and fix it.
stages.checkpoint: A fresh clone builds and runs correctly with no manual fixes beyond what's documented in the repo.

rubric.criterion: The project is actually live at a public URL
rubric.meets: Opening the URL in a browser, from a different device or network, shows the working project.

rubric.criterion: No secret is committed anywhere in the repo's history
rubric.meets: A search of the codebase and its commit history turns up no real API keys, passwords, or tokens — everything sensitive is an environment variable.

rubric.criterion: The build is reproducible from a fresh clone
rubric.meets: Cloning the repo somewhere new and running the documented build command works with no undocumented manual steps.

rubric.criterion: The output directory and build command are correctly configured
rubric.meets: The host is serving the actual current build output, not a stale or wrong folder — verified by making a small change and confirming it appears live.

contentSections.body: A live URL is the easy part — a build that reproduces cleanly from a fresh clone is the part that proves the deploy will still work in six months, on a different machine, without you there to fix it by hand.

title: Checkpoint — Deploying
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Debugging Properly, two reaching back into Organising a Project. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Deploying

questions.prompt: What three things does a hosting provider actually give you, together, that your own laptop usually can't reliably provide at the same time?

options.label: A computer that's on, publicly addressable, and actively running your code
A code editor, a terminal, and a debugger
A domain name, an email account, and a database

questions.explanation: Hosting means a machine that stays on, has a public address the rest of the internet can find, and is actively serving your code — your laptop can technically do all three, just not reliably, which is what you're really paying (or trading a free-tier limit) for.

questions.prompt: A deploy log shows the build succeeded, but the live page is completely blank. What's the most likely cause?

options.label: The host is configured to serve the wrong output directory
The build actually failed silently despite the success message
This is always a browser caching issue

questions.explanation: A build succeeding and being served correctly are separate facts — a blank page after a clean build almost always means the host is pointed at the wrong output folder.

questions.prompt: A real API key was hardcoded into a file, committed, and then deleted in the very next commit. Is the key still exposed?

options.label: Yes — it remains fully readable in the earlier commit's history until the key itself is revoked at the source
No — deleting the line in a later commit fully removes the exposure
Only if the repository is public, never if it's private

questions.explanation: Git history is history — every earlier commit remains fully accessible. Only revoking the actual credential at its source neutralizes an exposed key.

questions.prompt: What is a custom domain, cost-wise?

options.label: A yearly rental, roughly $10-15/year for a typical .com, separate from hosting cost
A one-time purchase, owned outright after the first payment
Always bundled free with any paid hosting plan

questions.explanation: A domain is rented per year from a registrar, a cost entirely separate from hosting — and it lapses, potentially permanently, if a renewal is missed.

questions.prompt: From Debugging Properly: why does making a fix before reliably reproducing a bug risk shipping a fix that doesn't actually work?

options.label: Without a reliable way to trigger the bug, there's no way to confirm the change addressed the real cause
It doesn't really risk anything — a reasonable-looking fix is generally enough
The only risk is that it takes longer, not that it might not work

questions.explanation: A bug you can't reliably reproduce is a bug you can't confirm you've fixed — any change is a guess with no way to verify it addressed the real cause.

questions.prompt: From Debugging Properly: roughly how many checks does halving the search space take to find one bad step among 50, compared to checking each one in order?

options.label: About 6 checks, versus up to 50 one at a time
Exactly the same number either way
It only works for sequences of exactly 10 or fewer

questions.explanation: Each check eliminates half the remaining possibilities, so 50 candidates narrow to 1 in roughly 6 checks — far fewer than checking every one in order.

questions.prompt: From Debugging Properly: sort logic that's textbook-correct still produces a wrong result on real data. What kind of bug is this usually?

options.label: A wrong assumption about the data's type, not a mistake in the logic itself
Always a syntax error the editor missed
Always a bug in the language's built-in sort function

questions.explanation: Rereading logic you're already confident is correct rarely helps when the real bug is a wrong assumption about the data feeding into it — like a string being treated as a sortable value.

questions.prompt: From Debugging Properly: why does a bug fix need a regression test, not just the fix itself?

options.label: Without a test, a later unrelated change could silently reintroduce the same bug with nothing catching it
A regression test is only needed for especially hard bugs
The fix alone is always sufficient — a test is a nice-to-have

questions.explanation: A fix without a test only solves the bug right now — a regression test, built from the real reproduction steps, is what keeps it solved against future changes.

questions.from: Three modules back — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: From Organising a Project: what's the point of separating configuration values that change per environment from the rest of the code?

options.label: So the same code can run correctly in development, testing, and production without being edited between them
It's purely a style preference with no functional benefit
It only matters for projects with more than one developer

questions.explanation: Values that differ per environment — a database address, an API key, a feature flag — belong outside the code itself specifically so the exact same code runs correctly everywhere it's deployed, which is the same principle this module's environment variables lesson builds directly on.

questions.from: Three modules back — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: From Organising a Project: what does a README need to let someone else actually do?

options.label: Run the project themselves, from a fresh clone, without asking the original author anything
Understand the author's full design reasoning for every file
Nothing specific — a README is mostly a formality

questions.explanation: A README's actual job is letting a stranger with a fresh clone get the project running with no other help — precisely the same standard this module's lab holds the deploy to.

contentSections.body: The link between this module and Organising a Project isn't a coincidence — a README someone else can follow and a build a fresh clone can reproduce are two versions of the same discipline.

title: Client and server: who does what
description: Every line of client-side code runs on a stranger's machine, fully visible and editable by them — the server is the one place code runs somewhere you actually control, which is the entire reason it exists.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the difference between code running on the client versus on the server
Identify why client-side logic can never be trusted to enforce a rule by itself

contentSections.title: Whoever runs the code controls the code

contentSections.body: A store's checkout page checks, in JavaScript, whether an item is still in stock before letting the "Buy" button submit. A curious visitor opens their browser's dev tools, finds the function doing that check, and simply calls it manually with a fake value — the button submits, whether or not the item is actually in stock, because the check was running on their own computer the whole time, not the store's.

contentSections.scenario: A JavaScript function in a checkout page: `function canPurchase(item) { return item.stock > 0; }`, called before allowing the order to submit. It runs entirely inside the visitor's browser, downloaded as part of the page.
contentSections.question: The visitor can open dev tools and call canPurchase() directly with any input they like, or just skip calling it and submit the order form some other way. What does that tell you about where this code actually runs?

options.label: It runs on the visitor's own machine, which means the visitor has complete control over it, not the store
It runs on the store's server, so the visitor's dev tools shouldn't be able to affect it
It runs somewhere in between, shared between both machines

feedback.client-controlled: Right. Client-side JavaScript is downloaded and executed entirely on the visitor's own machine — which means the visitor's browser, dev tools, and even a manually edited copy of the page are all fully in the visitor's control. Any check written only in that code is, functionally, a suggestion the visitor's own browser is trusted to enforce on itself.
feedback.server-controlled: If this were true, dev tools wouldn't be able to touch it at all — but they can, completely, because the function's actual code is sitting right there in the browser's memory, downloaded like any other file the page loaded.
feedback.shared: There's no in-between here — this specific function runs entirely client-side, full stop. A server-side check would be a separate piece of code, actually running on a machine the visitor has no access to, which is exactly what this lesson gets to next.

contentSections.concept: Client-side code — anything running in the browser, written in JavaScript that gets downloaded and executed on the visitor's own machine — is always under the visitor's control, no matter how it's written or hidden. Server-side code runs on a machine you (the developer) actually control, one the visitor never gets direct access to. The distinction isn't about which language is used; it's about whose machine the code actually executes on.

contentSections.body: This single fact is the entire reason a backend exists at all: anything that has to be actually true, actually enforced, actually trusted — inventory counts, prices, who's allowed to see what — has to be checked on a machine the requester doesn't control. The client can still *display* the stock check, for a fast, responsive interface; it just can never be the thing that's actually relied on to be true. The server, checked again independently, is what makes the rule real.

A useful habit going forward: anywhere client-side code says "if this, then that's allowed," ask the follow-up question — what happens if someone simply skips straight to "that"? If the honest answer is "nothing stops them, because nothing else checks," that's a rule that only exists as a UI convenience, not an actual guarantee, and anything genuinely important needs the same check repeated somewhere the client can't reach.

contentSections.scenario: A coupon code field on a checkout page: entering "SAVE20" runs a JavaScript function that subtracts 20% from the displayed total, purely client-side, with no request sent anywhere. The actual charge, when the order is submitted, goes through a separate server-side payment process.
contentSections.question: What's the actual risk in this setup, beyond the coupon just looking nice on screen?

options.label: Someone can edit the client-side code (or the page's variables directly) to apply a bigger discount than any real coupon offers, unless the server independently validates the coupon and recalculates the price itself
There's no real risk — the coupon logic is simple enough that it doesn't matter where it runs
The risk is only that the coupon might not be spelled correctly

feedback.bypassable: Right. If the discount is only ever calculated client-side, a visitor can change what number gets sent, or apply the discount function to any total they like, entirely on their own machine — and if the server just trusts whatever final price the client sends, it will charge whatever the visitor decided to submit. The fix is the server independently looking up the real coupon and recalculating the actual price itself, ignoring whatever number the client displayed.
feedback.no-risk: The simplicity of the logic has nothing to do with the risk — even a one-line discount calculation is fully visible and editable the moment it runs in the visitor's own browser. Complexity isn't what makes something trustworthy; where it runs is.
feedback.spelling: A misspelled coupon code is a minor UX annoyance, not the actual risk this scenario is pointing at — the real issue is whether the final price charged is ever independently verified somewhere the customer can't directly control.

contentSections.mechanism: Any value that determines something with real consequences — money changing hands, access being granted, data being deleted — has to be independently checked on the server, using the server's own trusted data (the real coupon list, the real stock count, the real account permissions), regardless of what the client displays or sends. The client's version of that value is a convenience for the interface; the server's version is the one that's actually enforced.

contentSections.body: Client-side code always runs on a machine the visitor controls — anything that needs to be actually true, not just displayed, has to be checked again on a server the visitor can't reach.

contentSections.title: A server is just a program that answers requests

contentSections.body: "Server" sounds like specialized hardware in a data center somewhere, and it can be — but at the level that matters for this module, a server is just a program, running continuously, that listens for incoming requests and sends back responses. It's code, the same as the client, just running in a place you control instead of a place the visitor controls.

The shape of almost every web interaction follows the same loop: a client (a browser, a mobile app) sends a request to a server, specifying what it wants; the server does whatever work is needed — checking a database, calling another service, running some logic — using data and code the client never sees; and the server sends back a response, usually as structured data (commonly JSON) or a rendered page. The client displays the response. Nothing about this loop requires the client to know *how* the server got its answer, only what the answer was.
A server is a program that listens for requests and answers them, using code and data the requester never has direct access to — that's the whole mechanism the rest of this module builds on.

title: Things that cannot happen in the browser
description: A short, specific list of things a browser genuinely cannot do safely or at all — charging a card, sending an email from your address, reliably enforcing a one-per-user limit — and why each one specifically requires a server, not just convention.

learningObjectives.text: Identify specific tasks that genuinely require a server, and explain why each one does

contentSections.title: Not everything needs a backend — but some things structurally can't avoid one

contentSections.body: A portfolio site with a contact form, a to-do list that saves to the browser's own storage, and a checkout flow that charges a real card are three very different projects — only one of them has a task that's genuinely impossible to do safely from the browser alone, no matter how it's written.

contentSections.scenario: Four features under consideration for a small project. Each either genuinely requires a server, or can be done entirely in the browser.
contentSections.question: Select every feature that genuinely, structurally requires server-side code — not just "is commonly built that way," but actually cannot be done safely from the browser alone.

items.label: Actually charging a customer's credit card
Sending a real email from the project's own address (not the visitor's own email client)
Reliably enforcing that a specific coupon can only be used once per account
Remembering a visitor's dark-mode preference between visits

explanation.charge-card: Charging a card requires a secret API key from a payment processor (Stripe and similar) — a credential that can never safely exist in browser code, since anything in the browser is visible to the visitor. The charge has to be initiated from a server holding that secret.
explanation.send-email: Sending email from a project's own address requires credentials for an email service, held server-side for the same reason — a visitor's browser has no legitimate, safe way to authenticate as your project's sender identity.
explanation.one-coupon-per-user: "Once per account" requires checking against a record of what's already happened, stored somewhere the visitor can't edit — the browser's own memory resets on every visit and is fully editable by the visitor, so it structurally cannot be the source of truth for a rule like this.
explanation.dark-mode: A visitor's own preference, remembered only for their own future visits, is a genuinely fine use of browser storage (localStorage) — nothing about it needs to be enforced against anyone, verified, or kept secret, so there's no structural reason it needs a server at all.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the three that need a server: each one involves either a secret credential that can't be exposed, or a rule that has to be true regardless of what the requester claims. The one that doesn't need a server involves neither — it's a convenience, remembered for the same person who set it, with nothing to protect and nothing to enforce against anyone else.

contentSections.body: A useful test, going forward: does this feature involve a secret (an API key, a password) that has to stay hidden from the person using the feature? Or does it involve a rule that has to hold true regardless of what the requester's own browser claims? If either is yes, it needs a server. If neither is true — it's just remembering or displaying something for the same person who set it — the browser alone is often completely sufficient, and adding a server would be unnecessary complexity for no real benefit.

A feature needs a server when it involves a secret that can't be exposed, or a rule that has to hold true regardless of what the requester's browser claims — otherwise, the browser alone is often genuinely enough.

contentSections.title: Costs and limits show up here too, not just in hosting

contentSections.body: A server-dependent feature isn't just a technical requirement — most of the services that make one possible (a payment processor, an email API, a database) have their own free tiers and their own specific costs once you're past them, the same way hosting did in the last module.

contentSections.scenario: A small project needs to send a confirmation email after signup. Two options: a transactional email API (like Resend or SendGrid) with a free tier around a few hundred emails a month, or a personal Gmail account's SMTP settings, reused for the project.
contentSections.question: For a small, real project actually meant to run reliably, which is the more sound choice, and why?

options.label: The transactional email API — built for exactly this, with a clear free-tier limit and predictable behavior once exceeded
Personal Gmail SMTP — free forever with no limits worth worrying about
Neither works reliably enough to matter — email delivery is unpredictable regardless of the sender

feedback.api: Right. A transactional email API is built specifically for this use case, publishes a clear free-tier limit (so you know exactly what happens as usage grows), and is designed for reliable, monitored delivery. It's the same category of decision as choosing a real host over running a server from a laptop — a purpose-built tool, with published, known limits.
feedback.gmail: A personal Gmail account has real, low, mostly-undocumented sending limits meant for one person's personal use, and using it for automated project email risks the account being flagged or throttled — "free forever with no limits" isn't actually true here, it's just less visibly limited until it suddenly is.
feedback.neither: Email delivery is a solved, reliable problem when done through a service built for it — the unpredictability specifically comes from using a tool (personal email) outside what it was ever designed or provisioned for, not from email as a category being inherently unreliable.

contentSections.concept: Just like hosting, most backend-adjacent services (email delivery, payment processing, file storage, databases) have real free tiers with published, specific limits, and real costs once you're past them. Choosing the purpose-built tool over a workaround (a real email API over a personal Gmail account, a real database over a text file) isn't about sophistication for its own sake — it's choosing something with known, predictable behavior at its limits over something with unknown, unpredictable behavior at its limits.

contentSections.body: Backend-dependent features usually lean on a purpose-built service with its own free tier and published limits — the same due diligence from choosing a host applies to choosing an email API, a payment processor, or a database.

title: Your first server endpoint
description: A server endpoint is a specific address the server listens on and answers — writing one, and calling it from the client, is the smallest complete round trip a real backend does.

learningObjectives.text: Write a minimal server endpoint that receives a request and returns a response
Call a server endpoint from client-side code and use its response

contentSections.title: The smallest possible round trip

contentSections.body: Everything about client-server communication, at its core, reduces to one small, complete loop: the client asks for something at a specific address, the server does something and answers, the client uses the answer. Stripped of every real-world complication, that loop is small enough to write in about ten lines.

contentSections.problem: Write the smallest possible server endpoint — one that receives a request at /api/hello and responds with a JSON greeting — and call it from client-side code.

steps.label: Define the endpoint on the server
steps.why: This tells the server: when a GET request arrives at exactly this address, run this function and send back this JSON object as the response. Nothing happens until a request actually arrives — the server is just listening.

steps.label: Call it from the client
steps.why: fetch() sends the actual request to that address. The server's function runs, sends back the JSON, and the client receives it, parses it, and can use it — here, just logging the message.

steps.label: Run both and watch the round trip happen
steps.work: Start the server, open the page in a browser, and watch the network tab: a request to /api/hello leaves the browser, and a response (with the JSON body) comes back a moment later.
steps.why: Seeing the actual request and response in the network tab is the concrete proof that this is a real client-server exchange, not something simulated locally — the response only exists because the server's code specifically ran and produced it.

faded.problem: Write and call a slightly different endpoint: /api/greet, which responds with a JSON object containing today's server time.

blanks.prompt: What does the server-side route definition need to specify, at minimum?
blanks.answer: The path (/api/greet) and a function that builds and sends a response
blanks.why: Every endpoint needs both an address to listen on and code that runs when a request arrives at that address.

blanks.prompt: What does the server actually send back?
blanks.answer: A JSON object, e.g. { time: new Date().toISOString() }
blanks.why: The response has to be something the client can parse and use — JSON is the common, structured choice for data (as opposed to a full HTML page).

blanks.prompt: What does the client-side code need to do with fetch()'s result before it's usable?
blanks.answer: Call .json() on the response to parse the body, then use the resulting object
blanks.why: fetch()'s raw response object isn't the data itself — .json() is what actually parses the response body into a usable JavaScript object.

contentSections.procedure: Define a route on the server (an address plus a function that builds and sends a response), and call it from the client with fetch(), parsing the response before using it. This is the same shape whether the response is one word or an entire database query's result.

contentSections.body: A server endpoint is an address plus a function that runs when a request arrives at it — the smallest real one is a handful of lines, and it's the exact same shape a full backend feature scales up from.

contentSections.title: The parts of a request that actually carry information

contentSections.body: The /api/hello example above ignores almost everything a real request can carry — but a request sent to search, submit a form, or log in needs to send information along with it, not just hit a bare address.

contentSections.question: A client needs to send a search term ("blue shoes") to the server and get back matching results. Put these into the order this actually happens:
steps: The client builds a request that includes the search term, e.g. as part of the URL: /api/search?q=blue+shoes
The server's route for /api/search reads the q value out of the incoming request
The server uses that value to look something up (in this lesson's case, hardcoded results; in the next lesson, a real database)
The server sends the results back as a JSON response
The client parses the JSON and displays the results
contentSections.explanation: The information travels with the request itself — as part of the URL here (a query parameter), or in the request's body for other kinds of requests (covered in the accounts module ahead). The server's job is reading that value out of the request it received, doing something with it, and sending a response; the client's job is building the request correctly and doing something useful with whatever comes back. Neither side needs to know how the other is implemented internally — only the shape of the request and response they've agreed on.

contentSections.body: This is the actual foundation the rest of the module builds on: a server can accept information from the client (search terms, form data, login credentials), do something with it using data and logic the client can't see, and send back a result — and every one of the trust boundaries from lesson one hold here specifically because that server-side function is running somewhere the client can't reach in or tamper with.

A request carries information with it — a query parameter, a body — and the server reads that information out, does something with it privately, and answers. This one small loop is the whole mechanism a real backend feature is built from.

title: Storing data somewhere permanent
description: A variable in a running server's memory disappears the moment that server restarts or redeploys — a database is what makes data actually survive, and choosing one for a small project is a much smaller decision than it sounds.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why data held in a server's memory does not survive a restart or redeploy
Identify when a project's data needs a real database rather than in-memory storage

contentSections.title: A variable is not a database, no matter how it feels while it's running

contentSections.body: A small to-do app stores its list in a plain JavaScript array on the server: `let todos = [];`. It works — adding, listing, deleting all function correctly — right up until the server redeploys (which lesson three of the deploy module showed happens on every single push) and the array resets to empty, silently, with every previously added to-do gone.

contentSections.scenario: A server holds its data in a plain variable, in memory, for the lifetime of the running process: `let todos = [];`, mutated as requests come in. The server itself is redeployed regularly — every push, per the deploy module — and can also restart on its own after a crash or a host-initiated maintenance restart.
contentSections.question: What happens to the data in that variable across a redeploy or restart?

options.label: It's completely gone — a fresh process starts with the variable back at its original, empty value
It's preserved automatically, since the code that recreates the variable is unchanged
It depends on how large the array has grown

feedback.gone: Right. In-memory storage lives entirely inside one running process. A redeploy or restart starts an entirely new process, running the code fresh from the top — `let todos = [];` runs again, producing a new, empty array, with zero connection to whatever was in the old process's memory. Nothing about the data was ever written anywhere that survives the process itself ending.
feedback.preserved: The code being unchanged is exactly why the data is lost, not why it's kept — `let todos = [];` runs again on every fresh process start, which is precisely the line that resets it to empty. Unchanged code re-run from scratch produces the same starting state every time.
feedback.depends-size: Size has nothing to do with it — an in-memory variable with one item or ten thousand behaves identically across a restart: gone entirely, because the entire process (and everything it was holding only in memory) ends and a new one begins.

contentSections.concept: Anything held only in a running process's memory — a plain variable, an in-memory array or object — exists only as long as that exact process keeps running. A restart, a redeploy, a crash: any of these start a fresh process with fresh memory, and nothing written only to the old process's memory carries over. Making data survive requires writing it somewhere that exists independently of any one running process — a file on disk that persists, or, for anything beyond the smallest toy project, a real database.

contentSections.body: A database is, at its simplest, exactly that: storage that exists independently of your server process, that your server connects to and reads from / writes to on every request that needs it. The server can restart as many times as it wants; the database keeps the data regardless, because it's a separate system entirely. For a small real project, a hosted database with a genuine free tier — options like a managed Postgres or a simpler hosted key-value store — is usually the right starting point: no server to maintain yourself, a real free allowance, and a clear, published limit for when a project outgrows it.

Anything stored only in a running process's memory disappears on the next restart or redeploy — a database is storage that exists independently of the server process, which is the entire property that makes data actually survive.

contentSections.title: When in-memory is genuinely fine, and when it isn't

contentSections.body: Not every server-held value needs to survive a restart — the deciding question is simply whether losing it on the next redeploy would actually matter to anyone.

contentSections.scenario: A small project's server holds several different things in memory. For each, consider what actually happens, and to whom it matters, if the server redeploys and that value resets.
contentSections.question: Select every one of these where losing the value on redeploy would be a real problem, worth moving to a real database.

items.label: A list of everyone who's signed up for the project
A user's saved to-do list items
A simple counter of how many requests the server has handled since it last started, shown on an internal debug page
A record of orders that have been placed and paid for

explanation.user-signups: Losing this on every redeploy means the project loses its actual users every time it's updated — a real, ongoing problem for anyone who signed up. This needs a real database.
explanation.todo-items: The entire value of a to-do app is that items persist — a redeploy silently deleting everyone's list defeats the app's basic purpose. This needs a real database.
explanation.request-counter: A counter that's explicitly framed as "since it last started" is honestly, correctly scoped to the current process's lifetime — resetting to zero on restart isn't a bug, it's exactly what the label already says it measures. In-memory is genuinely fine here.
explanation.orders: Losing paid order records on redeploy is a serious, real-world problem — financial records, fulfillment obligations, and customer trust all depend on this surviving. This needs a real database, without question.

contentSections.synthesis: The actual test is whether the value's meaning depends on surviving past the current process — a to-do list, user accounts, and orders are all supposed to persist by definition, so losing them is a real bug. A counter explicitly scoped to "this run" is honestly fine to lose, because losing it doesn't break what it was ever claiming to measure.

contentSections.body: The test isn't whether something is stored in memory — it's whether the value's whole meaning depends on surviving past the current process. If it does, it needs a real database, not a variable.

title: Keeping a secret actually secret
description: A secret key called from client-side code is visible to anyone who opens the browser's network tab or reads the shipped JavaScript, minified or not — a server acting as the only thing that ever touches the real key is what actually keeps it hidden.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a specific architecture actually keeps a secret key server-side

contentSections.title: Minified is not the same as hidden

contentSections.body: A learner, remembering the deploy module's rule about not committing secrets to Git, sets an API key as an environment variable — but the client-side code calls the third-party API directly, reading that variable and putting it straight into a fetch() request's headers. No secret was ever committed to Git. It's still fully exposed.

contentSections.question: The key is genuinely set as an environment variable, and never committed to Git anywhere. What's still wrong with this specific code?

options.label: This code runs in the browser, so the built, deployed JavaScript still contains the real key value, visible to any visitor who opens dev tools or the network tab
Nothing — environment variables are always safe, everywhere they're used
The only problem is that VITE_API_KEY is a poorly chosen variable name

feedback.still-client-visible: Right. An environment variable prefixed for a client-side build tool (like Vite's VITE_ convention) gets baked directly into the shipped JavaScript bundle at build time — it's not a runtime secret at all once deployed, it's plain text sitting in a file the browser downloads. Anyone can view the page source, or the network tab, and read the exact key value. Keeping it out of Git solved a completely different problem than keeping it out of the client.
feedback.fine: This is exactly the trap: the deploy module's Git rule is genuinely necessary but not sufficient on its own. An environment variable that ends up embedded in client-side, browser-shipped code is exposed the moment it's deployed, regardless of how carefully it was kept out of source control.
feedback.naming: The variable's name has nothing to do with the actual exposure — even a perfectly named variable, once its value is compiled into client-side JavaScript, is fully readable by anyone who opens the browser's dev tools.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix isn't a different way of storing the key — it's moving where the request happens at all. The client should call your own server endpoint (which holds the real key, safely, since server code never gets shipped to the browser); the server, in turn, calls the third-party API using the real key, and returns only the result to the client. The client never sees the key in any form, because it never touches code that runs on the client's own machine.

contentSections.body: This is the general shape for any secret a client-side app needs the *effect* of, without ever holding the key itself: the client calls your server; your server, using the key it holds safely, calls the actual third-party service; the server passes back only the useful result. This is often called proxying — the server sits between the client and the real API specifically so the real credential never has to leave server-controlled code.

An environment variable kept out of Git can still be fully exposed if it ends up embedded in client-side code — the actual fix is a server that holds the key and makes the request on the client's behalf, so the key never ships to the browser at all.

contentSections.title: The same idea, generalized

contentSections.body: This isn't specific to one API — it's the general answer to "how do I let my front end use something that needs a secret key" for practically any third-party service a project might integrate with.

contentSections.scenario: A project wants to let visitors generate an AI image from a text prompt, using a third-party image-generation API that requires a secret key per request.
contentSections.question: Where should the actual API call to the image-generation service happen?

options.label: On the project's own server, which holds the key and makes the call on the client's behalf, returning just the resulting image URL
Directly from the client, since it's simpler and avoids running a server at all
It doesn't matter, as long as the key is stored as an environment variable somewhere

feedback.server-proxy: Right. The project's own server is the one place the key can live without being exposed to every visitor — the client sends the prompt to the project's server, the server calls the image API using the real key, and sends back only the resulting image. The key never becomes part of anything shipped to the browser.
feedback.direct-client: Simpler in the short term, catastrophic in practice — a key embedded in client-side code is readable by any visitor, who could then use it themselves, potentially running up real charges against the project's own account.
feedback.doesnt-matter: Where an environment variable is *set* and where the code that *uses* it actually *runs* are two different questions — a key can be a perfectly well-managed environment variable and still end up compiled directly into client-shipped code if the code using it runs client-side, which is exactly last section's trap.

contentSections.mechanism: Any secret credential needs to live in code that runs only on infrastructure you control — which server-side code, by definition, is, and client-side code, by definition, is not. The general pattern (client calls your server, your server calls the third-party service using the key, your server returns the result) is the shape this takes for practically every integration that requires a secret: payments, email, AI APIs, and anything else with a key attached.

contentSections.body: Whenever a client-side feature needs something a secret key unlocks, the client calls your server, your server makes the real call and holds the key, and only the result comes back — the key itself never becomes part of anything the browser downloads.

title: Practice — Decide Client or Server for Eight Features
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a described feature, decide whether it can live entirely in the browser or genuinely requires a server, and why.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the client/server trust and secret-handling distinctions to unfamiliar features

contentSections.title: Eight decisions, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: whether client-side code can be trusted to enforce a rule, whether a feature involves a secret that can't be exposed, whether data needs to survive a restart, and whether a secret is actually kept server-side or just hidden.
The same real question every time: does this involve a secret that can't be exposed, or a rule that has to hold true no matter what the client claims?

title: Lab — Add a Small Backend to Your Project
