description: Add one real server endpoint to a real project, one that does something the client genuinely cannot do safely on its own — with its secret, if it has one, actually kept server-side, not just out of Git.

learningObjectives.text: Add a working server endpoint to a real project that the client calls for a real reason
Verify a secret used by the new endpoint never ships to the client

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick one real thing your project currently does entirely client-side that shouldn't be — or one new small feature that genuinely needs a server (calling a third-party API with a key, or storing something that needs to survive a restart) — and build the actual endpoint for it.

contentSections.title: Add a small backend to your project
contentSections.brief: Identify one feature in a real project of yours that genuinely needs a server — something involving a secret that can't be exposed, or a rule that has to hold true no matter what the client sends. Build the endpoint, call it from your front end, and verify the secret (if there is one) never ships to the browser.
contentSections.deliverable: A working endpoint your front end calls, with its secret kept server-side.

stages.title: Pick the feature and confirm it actually needs a server
stages.instructions: Using this module's test (does it involve a secret, or a rule that has to hold true regardless of what the client claims?), pick one real feature. Write one sentence stating specifically why it needs a server — not just "it's the standard way to build this."
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific feature and a one-sentence, specific reason it genuinely needs a server.

stages.title: Write the server endpoint
stages.instructions: Write the actual endpoint — a route that receives a request, does the real work (using a secret held as an environment variable if one is needed), and sends back a response. Test it directly first (a tool like curl, or the browser, for a GET endpoint), before wiring up the front end.
stages.checkpoint: Calling the endpoint directly returns the expected response.

stages.title: Call it from the front end
stages.instructions: Wire up the client-side code to call your new endpoint with fetch() (or your framework's equivalent), and use the response to actually do something visible — display data, show a confirmation, update the UI.
stages.checkpoint: The feature works end to end from the actual UI, not just when tested directly.

stages.title: Verify the secret never ships to the client
stages.instructions: If the endpoint uses a secret key, open your browser's dev tools — the Sources or Network tab — and confirm the key does not appear anywhere in the JavaScript sent to the browser, or in any request the browser itself sends. It should only ever appear in server-side logs, if anywhere.
stages.checkpoint: You have personally confirmed, by looking, that the real secret value appears nowhere in anything sent to the browser.

rubric.criterion: The feature genuinely required a server

rubric.criterion: The endpoint works correctly on its own
rubric.meets: Calling the endpoint directly (outside the UI) returns the correct response for at least one real input.

rubric.criterion: The feature works end to end from the actual UI
rubric.meets: A visitor using the real interface, not a developer testing the endpoint directly, sees the feature work.

rubric.criterion: The secret is verifiably never sent to the client

contentSections.body: A backend feature isn't done when it works — it's done when you've personally checked, in dev tools, that whatever needed to stay secret actually did.

title: Checkpoint — When You Need a Backend
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Deploying, two reaching back into Checking Your Own Work. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — When You Need a Backend

questions.from: This module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: A stock-check function runs entirely in client-side JavaScript. What does that mean about who actually controls it?

options.label: The visitor's own browser controls it fully — it can be inspected, edited, or bypassed from dev tools
The store's server controls it, since the store wrote the code
Control is shared between the browser and the server

questions.explanation: Client-side code runs entirely on the visitor's own machine, which means the visitor's browser and dev tools have full control over it, regardless of who originally wrote it.

questions.from: This module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: Which of these genuinely requires a server, structurally, not just by convention?

options.label: Reliably enforcing that a coupon can only be used once per account
Remembering a visitor's own dark-mode preference for their next visit
Displaying a countdown timer on a page

questions.explanation: A once-per-account rule requires checking against a record the visitor can't edit — the browser's own storage is fully editable by the visitor, so it can't be the source of truth for a rule enforced against that same visitor.

questions.from: This module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: Data held only in a running server's memory (a plain variable) — what happens to it on a redeploy?

options.label: It's gone entirely — a fresh process starts with the variable back at its original value
It's preserved, since the code that created it hasn't changed
It's preserved only if the redeploy is small

questions.explanation: A redeploy starts an entirely new process with fresh memory — anything held only in the old process's memory has no connection to the new one and is simply gone.

questions.from: This module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: An API key is kept out of Git successfully, but the client-side code reads it from an environment variable and puts it directly into a fetch() request. Is the key actually secret in production?

options.label: No — client-side environment variables get baked into the shipped JavaScript, fully visible in dev tools
Yes — keeping it out of Git is sufficient on its own
Only if the variable name doesn't obviously suggest it's a secret

questions.explanation: Keeping a key out of Git and keeping it out of client-shipped code are two separate problems — a client-side environment variable is compiled directly into the deployed JavaScript and fully visible to any visitor.

questions.prompt: From Deploying: a deploy log shows the build succeeded, but the live page is blank. What's the most likely cause?

options.label: The host is configured to serve the wrong output directory
The build must have actually failed despite the success message
This is always a browser caching issue

questions.explanation: A build succeeding and being served correctly are separate facts — a blank page after a clean build almost always means a misconfigured output directory.

questions.prompt: From Deploying: an API key is hardcoded, committed, then deleted in the very next commit. Is it still exposed?

options.label: Yes — it remains fully readable in the earlier commit's history until revoked at the source
No — the later deletion removes the exposure
Only if the repository is currently public

questions.explanation: Git history retains every earlier commit — the only fix for an already-exposed secret is revoking it at its source, not deleting the line later.

questions.prompt: From Deploying: roughly what does a standard .com domain cost per year?

options.label: Roughly $10-15/year at a typical registrar
A one-time fee of around $10-15, owned outright afterward
Always free with any hosting provider

questions.explanation: A domain is a yearly rental from a registrar, typically around $10-15/year for a standard .com, separate from hosting cost entirely.

questions.prompt: From Deploying: why does committing a project's build output (dist/) instead of letting the host build it create a hidden risk?

options.label: Every future source change now depends on someone remembering to manually rebuild and recommit, with no error if they forget
Git technically can't store built files
It has no downside — it's strictly simpler

questions.explanation: It trades a one-time setup cost for a permanent, invisible manual step — a missed rebuild silently ships stale code with nothing to catch the mismatch.

questions.from: Three modules back — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: what's the concrete way to prove a test would actually catch a real bug?

options.label: Temporarily break the code it tests and confirm the test fails, then revert and confirm it passes again
Give the test a longer, more detailed name
Run the same test twice in a row

questions.explanation: Watching a test go red on deliberately broken code, then green again on the real code, is the actual proof it checks something meaningful — the same proof-of-meaningfulness idea this module's lab applies to a checked-in-dev-tools secret.

questions.from: Three modules back — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: why is testing edge cases (empty input, the largest expected value) more valuable than re-testing the ordinary middle case repeatedly?

options.label: Ordinary cases are what a developer already checked by hand while writing the code — edges are where untested assumptions usually break
Edge cases are simply faster to write tests for
There's no real difference in value between the two

questions.explanation: A developer naturally exercises the ordinary case while writing and manually checking code — it's the edges (empty, largest, smallest, unexpected type) where an unstated assumption is most likely to have gone unchecked.

title: What an account really requires of you
description: "Add login" sounds like one feature — it's actually a standing commitment: securely handling credentials, recovering access when someone forgets, and being the place a person's data lives for as long as the account exists.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the ongoing obligations a login feature creates, beyond the initial signup form

contentSections.title: Signup is a form. An account is a standing commitment.

contentSections.body: A weekend project adds "Sign up / Log in" to its homepage — a form, a database table, done in an afternoon. Three months later: someone forgot their password and there's no reset flow, someone's email changed and there's no way to update it, and someone asks — reasonably — what happens to their data if they delete their account. None of that was in the original afternoon's work, and all of it is now owed.

contentSections.scenario: A project ships basic signup and login over a weekend: an email field, a password field, a database row created on signup, checked on login. Nothing else.
contentSections.question: Is shipping the signup/login form itself the completion of "adding accounts," or the start of an ongoing set of obligations?

options.label: The start — password reset, data export/deletion, and keeping the account secure over time are all now genuinely owed, not optional extras
The completion — once signup and login work, the feature is done
It depends entirely on how many users actually sign up

feedback.start: Right. The moment a real person creates an account with real credentials, several things become genuinely owed, not optional: a way to recover access if they forget their password, some path for them to see or delete their own data, and an ongoing responsibility to keep whatever's stored about them reasonably secure. None of these show up in a login form's happy path, and all of them show up the first time a real user hits the edge case.
feedback.done: The login form working is real progress, but "a user forgot their password" and "a user wants their data deleted" are not edge cases that might happen — for any account system with real users, they are eventually guaranteed to happen, and neither is handled by a working signup form alone.
feedback.depends: The number of users changes *when* these obligations get tested, not *whether* they exist — even a single real user creates the same underlying commitments (recoverability, data handling) the moment their account is created, whether or not the edge cases have come up yet.

contentSections.concept: Adding accounts to a project is not a single feature that gets finished — it's the start of an ongoing relationship with real people's credentials and data. The specific obligations this creates: a way to recover access without the original password, a clear answer to what happens to a person's data if they leave, and an ongoing duty to keep whatever's stored reasonably secure against a breach. A login form that handles only the happy path (successful signup, successful login) hasn't finished this — it's completed the smallest, easiest ten percent of it.

contentSections.body: This isn't a reason to avoid building login — most real projects genuinely need it. It's a reason to be honest, before building it, about what's actually being taken on: every account is a standing promise to a specific person that their access can be recovered, their data is handled with some care, and the whole system stays secure over the life of the project — not just on launch day. Lesson four covers the practical way most small projects meet this bar without building all of it from scratch.
Login isn't a feature that finishes when the form works — it's a standing commitment to recovery, data handling, and ongoing security for every real person who signs up.

contentSections.title: The questions worth asking before the first signup form

contentSections.body: Before writing a single line of login code, a short, concrete list of questions is worth more than most of the code itself — because the answers change what actually needs to be built.

contentSections.question: Put these questions in the order it actually makes sense to ask them, before building an account system:
steps: Does this project genuinely need accounts at all, or would something simpler (no login, or a single shared password) actually work?
What real data will be tied to an account, and what happens to it if the account is deleted?
How will someone recover access if they forget their password?
Who is actually going to build and maintain all of this over time?
contentSections.explanation: The first question is the one most often skipped entirely — plenty of small projects add login out of habit, when a simpler mechanism (no accounts at all, or one shared access code) would meet the actual need with none of the ongoing obligations from the first pod. Only once accounts are genuinely justified do the specifics (what data, what recovery, who maintains it) become the real questions — asking them in this order is what stops a small project from accidentally taking on a large, permanent commitment for a feature it didn't strictly need.

contentSections.body: A genuinely useful gut check: if the honest answer to "does this need real accounts" is "not really, but it seems standard," that's worth pausing on. A lot of small projects are better served by something much lighter — no login at all, a single shared link, or a simple access code — than by taking on the full, ongoing weight of real user accounts for a feature that didn't actually require them.
Ask whether accounts are genuinely needed before building them — the ongoing commitment from the first pod is only worth taking on when something simpler genuinely can't meet the real need.

title: Passwords: never storing what you don't have to
description: A password should never be stored as plain, readable text — hashing turns it into something that can be checked but never reversed, which means even a full database breach doesn't hand out anyone's actual password.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why passwords must be hashed rather than stored as plain text

contentSections.title: A breach should not mean handing out real passwords

contentSections.body: A database of user accounts gets breached — it happens, to companies of every size, regularly. If the passwords column contains actual, readable passwords, the breach hands the attacker every single one of them, ready to try on other sites where the same person reused that password. If the column contains a hash instead, the attacker gets something that can't be turned back into the original password at all.

contentSections.scenario: A password field is stored in the database exactly as the user typed it: `password: "correcthorsebatterystaple"`. Login works by comparing the typed password directly against this stored value.
contentSections.question: The login logic works correctly. What's the actual, specific danger here?

options.label: If the database is ever breached (or even just read by someone who shouldn't — an insider, a backup left exposed), every real password is immediately readable and reusable elsewhere
Nothing — as long as the database itself has a strong password protecting access to it
This is only a problem for very large, high-profile projects

feedback.readable: Right. Storing a password as plain, readable text means anyone who ever gains access to that data — through a breach, a misconfigured backup, an overly curious employee, a leaked database dump — gets the actual password, not just access to this one account. Since people commonly reuse passwords, this often compromises accounts on completely unrelated sites too.
feedback.db-password-enough: A strong database password is a real, worthwhile layer of protection, but it's one layer among several a real breach can get past — misconfigurations, leaked credentials, unpatched software, and insider access all bypass it. Plain-text passwords mean a breach that gets past that one layer is catastrophic instead of contained.
feedback.scale-only: Small projects are breached too, and a small project's users reuse the same passwords everywhere just as often as a large company's users do — the actual risk to each individual person doesn't shrink because the project itself is small.

contentSections.mechanism: The specific danger of plain-text password storage is that a single point of failure (one breach, one leak, one careless backup) exposes every user's actual password at once, in immediately reusable form. The fix, covered next, is to never store the actual password at all — only a one-way transformation of it that can verify a login attempt without ever being reversible back into the original.

contentSections.body: A password hash is the output of a one-way function: feed in the password, get back a fixed-length string that looks like random characters, and — this is the entire point — there is no practical way to run that function backwards and recover the original password from the hash. Login works by hashing whatever the user just typed and comparing that new hash against the stored one; if they match, the password was correct, without the system ever needing to know or store the actual password itself, before or after that comparison.
A password hash lets a login be verified without the system ever storing (or being able to recover) the actual password — a breach of the hashes doesn't hand out anyone's real password.

contentSections.title: Hashing a password is not the same as encrypting one

contentSections.body: Encryption and hashing sound similar and get confused constantly, but they solve genuinely different problems, and using the wrong one for a password is a real, specific mistake.

contentSections.scenario: Two mechanisms: encryption (scrambles data reversibly with a key — the same key, or a matching one, can turn it back into the original) and hashing (one-way — there is no key that turns a hash back into the original input).
contentSections.question: Select the true statements about storing a password using each.

items.label: An encrypted password can, in principle, be decrypted back to the original — by anyone who has (or steals) the key
A properly hashed password cannot be turned back into the original, even by the system that created the hash
Encryption is the right tool specifically for password storage, since it's more secure than hashing
A hashed password can still be checked against a login attempt, by hashing the attempt and comparing

explanation.encrypt-reversible: True, and this is exactly the property that makes encryption the wrong tool here — anyone who obtains the decryption key (through a breach, a leaked config, an insider) can turn every stored password back into its original, readable form.
explanation.hash-irreversible: True, and this is the property that actually matters for passwords — there should be no key, no shortcut, no way for anyone (including the system's own operators) to recover a real password from its stored hash.
explanation.encrypt-right-choice: False. Encryption is the right tool when the *original* value genuinely needs to be recovered later by someone with the key (an encrypted file, a message meant to be read again) — a password is never supposed to be recovered by anyone, which is exactly what makes hashing, not encryption, the correct tool.
explanation.hash-verifiable: True — this is the whole mechanism that makes hashing usable for login at all: hash the login attempt, compare it to the stored hash, and a match confirms the password was correct without either side ever needing the original value again.

contentSections.synthesis: Encryption answers "how do I store this so I (or someone with the key) can get the original back later" — the wrong question for a password. Hashing answers "how do I verify this was correct without ever being able to recover it" — exactly the right question, and exactly why every credible authentication system uses hashing, never encryption, for passwords specifically.

contentSections.body: Encryption is reversible by design — the wrong property for a password. Hashing is irreversible by design, letting a login be verified without the original password ever being recoverable, by anyone.

title: Sessions and staying logged in
description: HTTP itself has no memory between requests — a session token is what a server hands back after a successful login, and what the browser sends on every later request to prove it's still the same, already-authenticated person.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a server needs a session mechanism to keep a user logged in across separate requests
Trace how a session token moves between client and server after a successful login

contentSections.title: Every request arrives as a stranger, by default

contentSections.body: A user logs in successfully. They click to a second page. From the server's perspective, that second request is, by default, completely unconnected to the first — HTTP doesn't remember anything about who made the previous request. Without something specifically added to fix this, the user would have to "log in" again on literally every single click.

contentSections.scenario: A user submits correct login credentials. The server verifies the password hash matches and responds with success. The user then clicks a link to a second page, sending a completely separate HTTP request.
contentSections.question: Does the server, by default, know this second request came from the same person who just logged in successfully?

options.label: No — HTTP requests are independent by default, with nothing connecting this one to the earlier successful login unless something is specifically added
Yes — the server remembers who logged in successfully for as long as the process keeps running
Only if the two requests come from the same IP address

feedback.no-memory: Right. HTTP is stateless by design — each request is handled independently, with no built-in memory of any previous request, successful login included. Without a mechanism specifically added to bridge that gap, the second request looks, to the server, exactly like a request from someone who's never logged in at all.
feedback.auto-remembers: The server process staying alive doesn't automatically connect requests to a specific person — a running server handles requests from many different people, all at once, with nothing built in that tags one particular request as coming from one particular already-authenticated user.
feedback.ip-based: IP addresses are shared (many people behind one office or home network) and change (mobile networks, VPNs), so they're neither reliable nor intended as an identity mechanism — nothing about matching an IP address constitutes actually being logged in.

contentSections.concept: HTTP is stateless: every request is handled as if it's the first one ever made by that client, with no memory of anything earlier, login included. Making "staying logged in" work requires deliberately bridging that gap — the server has to hand the client something after a successful login that the client can send back on every later request, proving it's the same already-authenticated person without re-entering a password every time.

contentSections.body: The most common mechanism: after a successful login, the server creates a session — a record, usually stored in a database or cache, tying a random, unguessable token to that specific user's identity — and sends that token back to the browser, typically as a cookie. The browser then automatically includes that cookie on every later request to the same site. The server checks incoming requests for that cookie, looks up the session it identifies, and — if it's valid — treats the request as coming from whichever user that session belongs to, with no password re-entry needed.
HTTP has no memory between requests by default — a session token, created on login and sent back on every later request (usually via a cookie), is what actually keeps a user logged in.

contentSections.title: What happens when a session token leaks

contentSections.body: A session token is, functionally, a temporary stand-in for being logged in — which means anyone who gets hold of a valid one is, as far as the server can tell, that logged-in user, with no password required at all.

contentSections.problem: Reason through what a stolen, valid session token actually lets an attacker do, and what limits the damage.

steps.label: What the token proves to the server
steps.work: The server trusts a valid session token as proof of "this request is from the already-authenticated user this session belongs to" — nothing more is checked per request.
steps.why: This is the entire mechanism sessions rely on: the token itself is the proof, not a re-check of the original password.

steps.label: What an attacker with a stolen token can do
steps.work: Send requests carrying that token and be treated, by the server, exactly as that logged-in user — reading their data, taking actions as them — for as long as the session stays valid.
steps.why: The server has no way to distinguish a request carrying a stolen token from one carrying the legitimate user's own token; the token itself is the only thing being checked.

steps.label: What limits the actual damage
steps.work: Sessions are usually given an expiration (forcing re-login after some time), can be revoked server-side (immediately invalidating a specific session, e.g. on logout or a reported compromise), and are typically sent only over HTTPS with cookie flags that prevent JavaScript or other sites from reading them.
steps.why: None of these prevent a stolen token from working while it's valid — they limit the window and the ways it can realistically be stolen in the first place, which is the practical, layered defense actually used.

faded.problem: A project's sessions never expire, and are stored in a cookie readable by any JavaScript running on the page. Reason through the risk this creates.

blanks.prompt: What does 'never expire' mean for a token stolen months ago?
blanks.answer: It would still be fully valid and usable today
blanks.why: Without expiration, a session's usefulness to an attacker has no natural time limit at all.

blanks.prompt: What does a JavaScript-readable session cookie make easier for an attacker?
blanks.answer: Stealing the token via a script injected into the page (a cross-site scripting attack)
blanks.why: A cookie flag exists specifically to block JavaScript from reading it, closing off this exact attack path — omitting it leaves the token reachable by any script that ends up running on the page.

blanks.prompt: What's the combined effect of both issues together?
blanks.answer: A stolen token would work indefinitely, and would be easier to steal in the first place
blanks.why: Expiration limits the damage window; the cookie flag limits how the token can be stolen at all — removing both removes two separate, independent layers of defense at once.

contentSections.procedure: A session token is trusted proof of identity for as long as it's valid — expiration limits how long a stolen token stays useful, server-side revocation allows cutting one off immediately, and protective cookie flags limit how it can realistically be stolen in the first place. None of these make a session unstealable; together they limit both the odds of theft and the damage if it happens.

contentSections.body: A session token is trusted as proof of identity on its own — expiration, server-side revocation, and protective cookie flags don't make it unstealable, but they limit both how it can be stolen and how much damage a stolen one can do.

title: Using an existing auth service instead of building one
description: Password hashing, session management, reset flows and social login are a genuinely large, security-critical surface to build correctly from scratch — an existing auth service (with its own real free tier and real limits) usually gets a small project further, faster, and safer.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate the tradeoffs between building authentication from scratch and using an existing auth service

contentSections.title: Everything from lessons 2 and 3, correctly, at once

contentSections.body: Lessons two and three each covered one specific, narrow piece of authentication — hashing, sessions — and each one is already easy to get subtly wrong. A real login system needs both of those done correctly, plus password reset, plus (usually) email verification, plus often social login (Google, GitHub) — all at once, all security-critical, all needing to stay correct as the project changes.

contentSections.scenario: A small project's founder is deciding between two paths: build the full authentication system from scratch (hashing, sessions, password reset, email verification), or use an existing auth service (Auth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth, or similar) that provides all of this, with a free tier for smaller projects.
contentSections.question: For a small project without a dedicated security specialist on the team, which is generally the more sound starting choice, and why?

options.label: An existing auth service — the security-critical parts are already built, tested at scale, and maintained by people whose job is specifically getting this right
Building from scratch — it's always better to fully understand and control every part of a system you rely on
Neither matters much — authentication is simple enough that either approach is equally safe

feedback.existing-service: Right. Authentication is exactly the kind of problem where a small team's own from-scratch implementation is disproportionately likely to have a subtle, serious flaw — a slightly wrong hashing configuration, a session bug, a reset-flow vulnerability — that an established service, hardened by far more usage and scrutiny than one small project can replicate, has already found and fixed. This mirrors the hosting and email decisions from earlier modules: a purpose-built tool with real, published limits over a workaround with unknown risk.
feedback.from-scratch: Full understanding and control are genuinely valuable in general, but for security-critical code specifically, the value of "battle-tested by many more real attacks than any single small project will ever face" usually outweighs the value of "built and understood entirely in-house" — this is a case where more control is not automatically the safer choice.
feedback.doesnt-matter: Authentication has produced real, serious breaches from small, well-intentioned implementations getting one subtle detail wrong — it's genuinely one of the areas where the choice of tooling has an outsized effect on actual risk, not a case where the approach barely matters.

contentSections.concept: For a genuinely security-critical, easy-to-subtly-mess-up system like authentication, an existing, established service is usually the sounder default for a small project — not because building it yourself is impossible, but because the cost of a mistake is high, the surface area (hashing, sessions, reset, verification, social login) is large, and an established service has already absorbed far more real-world attack attempts and scrutiny than a new project's own implementation ever will.

contentSections.body: This isn't a rule against ever building auth yourself — a learning-focused, no-real-user project is a genuinely good place to build a basic version by hand, specifically to understand lessons two and three concretely rather than abstractly. It's a specific recommendation for anything with real users and real data: use an established service, and spend the saved time on the actual product.

Authentication is large, security-critical surface area that's easy to get subtly wrong — for a project with real users, an established auth service is usually the sounder default, saving the from-scratch build for learning projects specifically.

contentSections.title: Real costs, real limits, same due diligence as every other service

contentSections.body: Like hosting and email, auth services have real free tiers with specific, published limits — usually based on monthly active users — and real costs once a project genuinely grows past them.

contentSections.scenario: A typical auth service aimed at small and growing projects, with a free tier meant to cover early-stage use.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many monthly active users does a typical free tier for an auth service like this cover, before paid pricing kicks in?
contentSections.explanation: Exact numbers vary a lot by provider and change over time, but many land somewhere in a low-thousands-to-tens-of-thousands range for a genuinely usable free tier — comfortably enough for a small real project to launch and grow on for a while before paid pricing becomes relevant. The specific number matters less than the habit: read the free tier's actual limit before relying on a service, the same as with hosting and email, so growth past it is an expected, planned-for milestone rather than a surprise.

contentSections.body: The due diligence is identical to every other third-party service in this track: what's included in the free tier, what specifically happens once it's exceeded (a hard block, a bill, a downgrade), and whether the specific provider's pricing model (often per monthly active user, sometimes per feature) fits how the project is actually expected to grow. None of this changes the lesson's core recommendation — it's the same evaluation applied to one more category of service.
An auth service's free tier has real, specific limits — usually scaled to monthly active users — worth reading once, the same due diligence already applied to hosting and email in earlier modules.

title: The data you are now responsible for
description: The moment a real account holds a real person's email, and anything else tied to it, that data is now something you're responsible for protecting, disclosing honestly, and eventually deleting on request — a responsibility that exists regardless of project size.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate what a specific project's account system makes the developer responsible for

contentSections.title: Small project, same underlying responsibility

contentSections.body: A side project with twelve users, all friends, feels informal — surely the rules that apply to a real company's user data don't really apply here. The data itself doesn't know the project is small: an email address, stored in a database with the same weak protections a hobby project might have, is exactly as real, and exactly as capable of being breached and misused, as one stored by a company with a full security team.

contentSections.scenario: A hobby project with a handful of real user accounts — real email addresses, hashed passwords, whatever else the signup form collected.
contentSections.question: Select every responsibility that genuinely applies here, small and informal as the project is.

items.label: Taking reasonable, real steps to protect that data from a breach (hashed passwords, not committing secrets, a reasonably secured database)
Being honest about what data is actually being collected and roughly why, even informally
Having some real way for a user to get their account and data deleted if they ask
None of the above genuinely applies, since the project is small and informal

explanation.protect-data: The size of the project has no bearing on whether the data itself is real and breachable — the same hashing, secret-handling, and reasonable security practices from earlier lessons apply regardless of how many users there are.
explanation.honest-about-collection: Even a completely informal project owes its users a basic, honest account of what's being collected — this doesn't require a legal document, but it does require not silently collecting more than what's obviously happening, or using it in a way the user wouldn't expect.
explanation.deletion-path: A user asking "can you delete my account" is a completely reasonable, foreseeable request the moment real accounts exist — having some real, working way to honor it (even a manual one, for a very small project) is part of the same standing commitment from lesson one.
explanation.size-exempts: Project size changes the scale of the risk and the formality of the response, not whether the underlying obligations exist at all — twelve real people's real data is still twelve real people's real data.

contentSections.synthesis: None of this scales down to zero just because a project is small — it scales down to something *simpler*, not something *absent*. A twelve-user hobby project's version of "data responsibility" might be a manually-run deletion script and a one-paragraph note about what's collected, rather than a formal privacy policy and an automated data-export tool — but the underlying obligations from lesson one (recoverability, honest data handling, security) are still real, just met at a scale appropriate to the project.

contentSections.body: A useful low-effort standard for a small project: write, honestly, in one or two sentences, exactly what's collected and roughly why — even just in a README or a short note on the signup page. If asked, actually be able to delete a specific user's data, even manually. Store passwords hashed, keep secrets out of Git and out of client code (both from earlier modules), and don't collect anything you don't have an actual reason to collect. None of this requires legal expertise or a formal policy — it requires taking the underlying commitment from lesson one seriously at whatever scale the project actually is.

Data responsibility scales down to something simpler for a small project, not to something absent — real people's real data still means real, if modest, obligations around protection, honesty, and deletion.

contentSections.title: What actually changes as a project grows

contentSections.body: The gap between a twelve-friend hobby project and a real product with paying strangers isn't a gap in whether these responsibilities exist — it's a gap in how much they're allowed to stay informal.

contentSections.question: As a project grows from a handful of friends to real strangers signing up, put these in the order they typically become genuinely necessary (rather than optional/informal):
steps: An honest, informal note on the signup page about what's collected and why
A real, working (even if manual) way to delete a user's data on request
A written privacy policy stating what's collected, how it's used, and how to request deletion
Formal compliance with a specific regulation (like GDPR or CCPA), if the project is subject to one based on where its users are
contentSections.explanation: The earliest, cheapest steps (honesty, a real deletion path) are worth doing from day one, regardless of scale — they cost little and are already the right thing to do. A written, public privacy policy becomes genuinely necessary once strangers (not just friends who already trust the project informally) are signing up, since they have no other way to know what's happening with their data. Formal regulatory compliance becomes a real, specific requirement once a project's user base and jurisdiction actually trigger it — a threshold worth knowing about before it's crossed, not after.

contentSections.body: None of this needs to be figured out fully before shipping a small first version — but knowing that the obligations grow, in this order, as the project grows, is what prevents "we'll deal with privacy stuff later" from becoming "we never dealt with it and now have real users we've made real, unmet promises to."

The obligations don't appear suddenly at some size threshold — they start small and informal from the very first real signup, and grow into something more formal as the project grows into real strangers' trust.

title: Checkpoint — Users and Accounts
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from When You Need a Backend, two reaching back into Version Control. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Users and Accounts

questions.prompt: Beyond the signup form itself, what does adding real accounts genuinely commit a project to?

options.label: Password recovery, some handling of user data on request, and ongoing security — not just a working login form
Nothing beyond the working signup and login forms
Only a written privacy policy, and nothing else

questions.explanation: A working login form covers only the happy path — recovery, data handling, and ongoing security are real, standing obligations the moment a real account exists.

questions.prompt: Why must a password be hashed, not encrypted, for storage?

options.label: Hashing is one-way and irreversible, so a breach can't recover anyone's actual password — encryption is reversible by design, the wrong property here
Encryption is simply an older, outdated technique compared to hashing
There's no real difference — either works equally well for passwords

questions.explanation: Encryption is reversible by anyone with the key — exactly the wrong property for a password. Hashing is irreversible by design, letting login be verified without the original ever being recoverable.

questions.prompt: Why does a server need a session mechanism to keep someone logged in?

options.label: HTTP is stateless — each request is handled independently, with no built-in memory of an earlier successful login
The server automatically remembers who logged in, as long as it keeps running
Sessions are only needed if the user is on a slow connection

questions.explanation: HTTP has no memory between requests by default — a session token, created on login and sent on every later request, is what bridges that gap.

questions.prompt: For a small project with real users but no dedicated security specialist, what's usually the sounder authentication choice?

options.label: An existing, established auth service, rather than building hashing, sessions, and reset flows from scratch
Building it fully from scratch, since that gives complete control
It doesn't matter much either way for a small project

questions.explanation: Authentication is large, security-critical surface area that's easy to get subtly wrong — an established service has absorbed far more real scrutiny than a new project's own implementation typically will.

questions.from: Previous module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: From When You Need a Backend: a stock-check runs entirely in client-side JavaScript. Who actually controls it?

options.label: The visitor's own browser — it can be inspected, edited, or bypassed from dev tools
The store's server, since the store wrote the code
Nobody — client-side checks are unbreakable by design

questions.explanation: Client-side code runs entirely on the visitor's own machine, fully under their control regardless of who wrote it.

questions.from: Previous module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: From When You Need a Backend: what happens to data held only in a server's in-memory variable, across a redeploy?

options.label: It's gone entirely — a fresh process starts with the variable back at its original value
It's preserved automatically, since the code is unchanged
It depends on how recently it was modified

questions.explanation: A redeploy starts an entirely new process with fresh memory — nothing held only in the old process's memory carries over.

questions.from: Previous module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: From When You Need a Backend: an API key is kept out of Git, but read directly by client-side code and sent in a request header. Is it actually secret in production?

options.label: No — client-side environment variables get baked into the shipped JavaScript, fully visible in dev tools
Yes — keeping it out of Git is sufficient
Only if the API doesn't use HTTPS

questions.explanation: Keeping a key out of Git and keeping it out of client-shipped code are separate problems — a client-side environment variable is compiled directly into the deployed bundle, fully visible to any visitor.

questions.from: Previous module — When You Need a Backend
questions.prompt: From When You Need a Backend: what's the correct pattern when a client-side feature needs something only a secret key can unlock?

options.label: The client calls your own server, the server holds the key and makes the real call, and returns only the result
The client calls the third-party API directly, using the key from an environment variable
It's fine either way, as long as HTTPS is used

questions.explanation: The key must live only in code that runs on infrastructure you control — server-side, by definition — with the client only ever talking to your own server.

questions.prompt: From Version Control: what does git reset --hard do to uncommitted changes in the working directory?

options.label: Discards them, related or not, with no automatic backup
Leaves them completely untouched
Automatically commits them before resetting

questions.explanation: "Hard" forces the working directory to match the target commit, silently discarding any uncommitted work in its path.

questions.prompt: From Version Control: what's the actual benefit of pushing a project's repository somewhere beyond your own laptop?

options.label: The project's history survives even if the one laptop holding it is lost, damaged, or stolen
It's purely a convenience for viewing code in a browser
It has no real benefit beyond satisfying a convention

questions.explanation: A repository that exists only on one machine is one hardware failure away from a project's entire history disappearing — pushing it elsewhere is a real, meaningful backup, not just a formality.

contentSections.body: Deploying got the project live. A backend made specific things trustworthy. This module made a specific promise to the actual people who sign up — the next module is about keeping that promise for months after launch, not just on day one.

title: Knowing it broke before a user tells you
description: A user reporting that your site has been down for two days is the worst possible way to find out — some form of monitoring, even a genuinely simple one, is what turns "someone eventually complains" into "you already know and are already fixing it."

learningObjectives.text: Explain why relying on user reports as the primary way to detect an outage is a real problem
Set up basic uptime monitoring for a deployed project

contentSections.title: The worst way to find out is a user telling you

contentSections.body: A side project's database connection quietly breaks on a Tuesday. Nobody notices — there's no error visible to the developer, nothing crashes loudly, the site just returns errors to anyone who visits. Four days later, a user finally comments "hey, your site's been broken all week" — and only then does the developer find out, four days after it actually happened.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways a developer could find out their project is down: (A) a user eventually notices and says something, at some unknown point after the outage started, or (B) an automated check visits the site every few minutes and sends an alert the moment it stops responding correctly.
contentSections.question: What's the actual, structural difference between these two, beyond speed?

options.label: (A) depends entirely on someone caring enough to report it, and has no guaranteed timeline at all; (B) is reliable and roughly bounded in how long an outage goes unnoticed
They're functionally the same, just different speeds of the same mechanism
(A) is actually more reliable, since real users notice real problems better than automated tools do

feedback.structural-diff: Right. Relying on a user report isn't just slower — it has no floor at all. A project with low traffic, or users who simply shrug and leave without saying anything, might stay broken for days or weeks with the developer never finding out through this channel. An automated check, run on a fixed schedule, bounds the maximum time an outage can go unnoticed to roughly that schedule's interval — a structurally different, reliable guarantee.
feedback.same-mechanism: The two aren't the same mechanism at different speeds — one has genuinely no upper bound on detection time (a broken site with quiet users could stay broken indefinitely, undetected), while the other has a real, predictable one.
feedback.a-better: A real user reporting a real problem is useful information, but as the *primary* detection mechanism it fails silently and often — many users simply leave a broken site without ever telling anyone, which an automated check doesn't depend on at all.

contentSections.concept: Waiting for a user to report an outage isn't a slower version of monitoring — it's structurally unreliable, with no guaranteed upper bound on how long a real outage can go completely unnoticed. An automated check, visiting the site on a fixed schedule and alerting on failure, bounds that detection time to something predictable and short, independent of whether any user happens to say anything.

contentSections.body: The actual tool for this is called uptime monitoring, and the free tier version is genuinely simple: a service (UptimeRobot, Better Uptime, and several others have real free tiers) visits a specific URL on your site every few minutes, and if it stops getting a normal response, it sends an alert — email, text, or a notification to wherever you actually check. Setting this up for one URL takes about five minutes and turns "I have no idea if my project is currently up" into "I'll know within minutes if it isn't."
Waiting for a user to report an outage has no real time limit — it might never happen. Automated uptime monitoring bounds detection time to minutes, for about five minutes of setup.

contentSections.title: What to actually watch, beyond "is it up at all"

contentSections.body: A site can return a normal-looking response while something underneath it is genuinely broken — a page that loads fine but a form that silently fails to submit, or an API that responds instantly with an error instead of the expected data. "Is it up" is the coarsest possible check, and it's a real, useful start, but it isn't the whole picture.

contentSections.scenario: A small project with a homepage, a signup form that posts to a server endpoint, and a scheduled task that sends a daily digest email. Several monitoring options are on the table.
contentSections.question: Select every one of these that would actually catch something a basic "does the homepage load" check would miss.

items.label: A monitor specifically checking that the signup endpoint returns success for a real test submission
An error-tracking tool that alerts when the server code throws an unexpected error, even if the page still loads
Just the basic homepage-loads check, run more frequently
A check confirming the daily digest email job actually ran and sent something, not just that it's scheduled

explanation.form-endpoint: A homepage loading correctly says nothing about whether a specific, separate endpoint (the signup form) is actually working — testing that endpoint directly catches a failure the homepage check would miss entirely.
explanation.error-alerting: A page can render a normal-looking response to the visitor while the server code behind a specific action is throwing errors — error tracking catches problems that never show up as an obviously broken page.
explanation.homepage-only: Checking the same one thing more often doesn't catch problems in things it was never checking in the first place — frequency doesn't substitute for coverage.
explanation.digest-confirmation: A scheduled task can be configured correctly and simply fail to run, or run and silently error out, with the homepage looking completely normal the entire time — a check confirming the job's actual output, not just its schedule, is what catches this.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern: "is the homepage up" only tells you about the homepage. Anything else the project genuinely depends on — a specific endpoint, a scheduled job, error rates on server code — needs its own, specific check, because a completely normal-looking homepage tells you nothing about any of them.

contentSections.body: "Is the homepage up" is a real, useful start, but it only tells you about the homepage — anything else the project depends on (an endpoint, a scheduled job) needs its own specific check.

title: Logs, and what to put in them
description: A log that says "error occurred" is barely more useful than no log at all — a genuinely useful log entry tells future-you what was happening, with enough specific detail to actually diagnose the problem without being there when it happened.

learningObjectives.text: Write a log message with enough specific detail to actually diagnose a problem later

contentSections.title: "Error occurred" tells future-you almost nothing

contentSections.body: A production error happens at 3am. The only log line is `console.error("error occurred")`. Three days later, trying to figure out what actually went wrong, that log line offers exactly nothing beyond confirming that something, at some point, went wrong — which was already known from the alert.

A log entry earns its place by answering, as specifically as possible, what future-you (or a teammate) would actually need to diagnose the problem without having been there: what operation was being attempted, with what specific input or identifier, and what exactly went wrong. `console.error("error occurred")` fails all three. Something like `console.error("Failed to send confirmation email for order #4821: SMTP connection timed out after 10s")` answers all three in one line — what was happening (sending a confirmation email), which specific case (order #4821), and what exactly failed (an SMTP timeout, not a vague "error").

contentSections.question: This code does log something on failure, and does respond with an error status. What's actually missing from the log line itself?

options.label: Any specific detail at all — which order, what operation, what the actual error was — making the log line nearly useless for diagnosing anything later
Nothing is missing — logging "error" is sufficient once an alert has already flagged that something is wrong
The problem is only that console.log was used instead of console.error

feedback.no-specifics: Right. `console.log("error")` confirms that something failed, which an alert or a 500 status already communicates — it adds no information about what was being attempted, which specific request or order, or what the actual underlying error was. Diagnosing this later means starting from nothing but a timestamp.
feedback.sufficient: Knowing *that* something failed and knowing *what actually failed and why* are very different amounts of information — an alert already tells you the former; a genuinely useful log line is what's supposed to supply the latter.
feedback.wrong-method: Using console.log instead of console.error affects how the line is categorized in some logging setups, but it's a much smaller issue than the log line containing zero actual diagnostic information regardless of which method wrote it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A useful version of this catch block logs the actual error object (which usually includes a real message and stack trace) along with the specific context — which order, which operation: `console.error(\`Failed to process order ${req.body.orderId}:\`, err);`. This one change turns a completely blank diagnostic trail into a specific starting point for figuring out what actually happened.

contentSections.body: A log line earns its place by answering what was happening, for which specific case, and what exactly went wrong — "error occurred" answers none of the three.

contentSections.title: Logging too much has its own real cost

contentSections.body: The instinct, once "log more detail" clicks, is to log everything — but a firehose of low-value log lines makes the one genuinely useful line, the moment it matters, harder to find, not easier.

contentSections.scenario: A server logs every single request it receives, with full headers and body, at a rate of several hundred lines per minute on a busy day — including for routes that never fail and carry no useful diagnostic value.
contentSections.question: A real error happens. What does this logging setup actually cost, at the moment it matters most?

options.label: The genuinely useful error log line is now buried in thousands of routine, low-value lines, making it harder and slower to actually find
Nothing — more logging is strictly better, since it can't hurt to have more information available
The only real cost is a slightly higher storage bill

feedback.buried: Right. Logging everything, indiscriminately, doesn't make the useful signal easier to find — it makes it harder, because the actual error is now one line among thousands of routine ones a person (or a search) has to sift through at exactly the moment speed matters most. Volume without judgment is a real cost, not a free safety net.
feedback.nothing: More logging has a real, specific cost at the exact moment it's supposed to help: finding the one useful line during an actual incident becomes slower, not faster, when it's surrounded by thousands of routine ones.
feedback.storage-only: Storage cost is real but usually the smaller problem — the bigger cost is to a human (or an automated search) trying to find the one line that matters during an actual live incident, buried in noise.

contentSections.mechanism: Useful logging is deliberate, not exhaustive: log the things that would actually help diagnose a real problem (errors, with specific context; meaningful state changes; the start and end of genuinely risky operations), and skip routine, always-succeeds operations that add volume without adding diagnostic value. The goal is a log that's small enough to actually search through during a real incident, and specific enough that the line you need says something useful when you find it.

contentSections.body: Logging everything indiscriminately buries the one useful line under thousands of routine ones — useful logging is deliberate about what actually deserves a line, not exhaustive.

title: Dependency updates and the ones that matter
description: Most dependency updates are genuinely low-risk and worth doing regularly — the ones that carry real risk are the specific ones (a major version bump, a security advisory) that need actual attention, not the same treatment as the rest.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a routine dependency update from one that carries real risk and needs deliberate attention

contentSections.title: Not all version bumps are the same kind of update

contentSections.body: A project's dependencies show 40 available updates. Treating all 40 the same way — either updating all of them blindly, or ignoring all of them out of caution — misses the real, useful distinction: most of them are genuinely low-risk, and a small number carry real risk worth actually paying attention to.

contentSections.scenario: Semantic versioning (semver) numbers a package as major.minor.patch — e.g. 3.1.4. A patch update (3.1.4 → 3.1.5) is meant for bug fixes with no intended behavior change. A minor update (3.1.4 → 3.2.0) adds new functionality without breaking existing usage, by convention. A major update (3.1.4 → 4.0.0) is explicitly allowed to break existing usage.
contentSections.question: Given what each version number is meant to signal, which kind of update carries the most real risk of breaking a working project?

options.label: A major update — it's explicitly allowed, by the convention itself, to change or remove things the project currently depends on
A patch update — bug fixes are inherently the riskiest kind of change
All three carry identical risk, since any code change could theoretically break something

feedback.major: Right. Semver's whole point is signaling exactly this: a major version bump is the explicit, agreed-upon signal that something the project currently relies on might have changed or been removed. Patch and minor updates carry real but much smaller risk, precisely because the convention promises they won't intentionally break existing usage.
feedback.patch: A patch update is specifically meant to fix a bug without changing intended behavior — genuinely the lowest-risk category by convention, which is exactly why routinely applying patch updates is usually safe.
feedback.identical: Semver exists specifically to make this distinction meaningful rather than theoretical — while no convention is perfectly followed 100% of the time, treating a patch bump with the same suspicion as a major version bump ignores real, useful signal the version number is deliberately providing.

contentSections.concept: Semantic versioning gives a real, if imperfect, signal about risk: patch updates (bug fixes, no intended behavior change) are usually safe to apply routinely; minor updates (new functionality, meant to be backward-compatible) are usually safe but worth a quick skim of what's new; major updates (explicitly allowed to break things) are the ones that deserve actual, deliberate attention — reading the changelog, testing before deploying, not just accepting the update automatically.

contentSections.body: A workable routine: patch and minor updates can often be applied on a regular schedule (weekly or monthly) with a quick test run afterward, since the risk is genuinely low by convention. A major update is worth pausing on specifically: read what changed, check whether anything the project actually uses is affected, and test deliberately before deploying — treating it with the same casual routine as a patch bump is where "I updated a dependency and it broke" actually happens.
Patch and minor updates are usually safe to apply routinely, by convention — a major update is the one that deserves actual, deliberate attention, since it's explicitly allowed to break things.

contentSections.title: The update that isn't optional: a security advisory

contentSections.body: Separate from the routine major/minor/patch schedule, a specific kind of update carries urgency none of the others do: a dependency with a known, published security vulnerability, where staying on the old version is an active, ongoing risk, not just neglect.

contentSections.scenario: A project runs `npm audit` (or the equivalent for its package manager) and finds a dependency with a published, high-severity vulnerability that a fixed version already exists for.
contentSections.question: Roughly how much delay, from discovering a fix already exists for a high-severity vulnerability, is reasonable before applying it, for a project taking this seriously?
contentSections.explanation: For a genuine high-severity vulnerability with a fix already available, the reasonable delay is close to zero — hours to a couple of days, mainly to actually test the update rather than to deliberate about whether it's worth doing. This is categorically different from the routine major/minor/patch schedule from earlier in the lesson: a known, published, fixable vulnerability is an active, specific risk with a known remedy sitting right there, not a general maintenance task competing for priority with everything else.

contentSections.body: Most package managers have a built-in audit command (`npm audit`, `pip-audit`, and similar) that checks installed dependencies against a database of known vulnerabilities — running it periodically (or having it run automatically in CI) is what actually surfaces this category of update instead of it silently sitting there. The routine schedule from the first pod handles ordinary maintenance; a security advisory jumps the queue entirely, precisely because the risk of *not* updating is active and specific, not general.

A published security vulnerability with a known fix isn't part of the routine update schedule — it's an active, specific risk that deserves near-immediate attention, checked for with a built-in audit command.

title: Coming back to your own project after eight weeks
description: Eight weeks away is long enough to have genuinely forgotten why a specific decision was made — a short, deliberate re-orientation routine gets you back to productive faster than diving straight into changing code you don't currently remember.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a re-orientation routine to a project you haven't touched in weeks or months

contentSections.title: You are, functionally, a new contributor to your own project

contentSections.body: Eight weeks is a genuinely long time, especially with the kind of variable capacity this whole track is built around — long enough that a specific, deliberate decision from two months ago (why is this endpoint checking a flag that seems to do nothing?) is completely gone, replaced with nothing. Diving straight into changing code under those conditions is exactly how a two-month-old, forgotten-but-load-bearing decision gets accidentally undone.

contentSections.question: Coming back to a project after eight weeks away, is the most productive first move usually to start making the change you had in mind, or to spend a few minutes re-orienting first?
contentSections.hint: Think about the Reading Other People's Code module — the same logic applies when the "other person" who wrote it is you, eight weeks ago.
contentSections.answer: Re-orienting first, briefly. Eight weeks is genuinely long enough that specific decisions, context, and half-finished threads are forgotten, not just fuzzy — functionally, you're returning to this code with close to the same blind spots the Reading Other People's Code module described for genuinely unfamiliar code. A few minutes spent re-orienting (reading the README, checking recent commits, running the project) before touching anything is what prevents accidentally undoing a decision you can no longer remember making.

contentSections.body: A short, repeatable routine, worth genuinely running rather than skipping past because "it's my own project, I basically remember it": read the README (and update it if it's stale — a stale README is a signal something changed without documentation keeping up); look at the last several commits and their messages to reconstruct what was actually being worked on; run the project locally and confirm it still starts and works at all before changing anything; and check for anything left obviously unfinished — a TODO comment, a half-written function, an open but stale branch.

Eight weeks away is long enough to be, functionally, a new contributor to your own project — a few minutes of deliberate re-orientation before touching code is what prevents accidentally undoing a decision you no longer remember making.

contentSections.title: Writing for the you who comes back in eight weeks

contentSections.body: The re-orientation routine works far better when past-you left something to re-orient with — which turns this lesson into a habit worth building now, for a return trip that hasn't happened yet.

contentSections.question: Before stepping away from a project for an extended, unplanned break, put these in the order they'd actually help a future return the most:
steps: Commit and push any in-progress work, even if it's incomplete, rather than leaving it uncommitted on disk
Write a short note (in the README, a commit message, or an issue) about what was being worked on and why
Make sure the project actually runs from a fresh clone, the same standard from the deploy module's lab
Leave any genuinely half-finished thought as an explicit TODO or open issue, not silent, unstated intent
contentSections.explanation: None of these are about finishing the work before stepping away — they're about making the state of things legible to someone (future-you) who won't remember the context. Committed, pushed work survives a laptop failure and is visible to re-orient from; a short note answers "what was I even doing" directly instead of relying on memory; a fresh-clone-runs check means the re-orientation routine's third step actually works when it's needed; and an explicit TODO beats a half-finished thought that only ever existed in your head at the time.

contentSections.body: This is the same discipline from the deploy and organizing-a-project lessons, aimed specifically at a different reader: not a stranger cloning the repo, but you, in eight weeks, having forgotten almost everything about the current state of things. The investment is small — a few minutes before stepping away — and it's what makes the re-orientation routine from the first pod actually fast instead of a genuine investigation.
Leaving a project genuinely legible before stepping away — committed work, a short note, a working fresh clone — is what makes the return trip's re-orientation routine actually fast.

title: Deciding to turn something off
description: Not every project deserves to stay running forever — a project with no real users, quietly costing money or attention, is a genuine candidate for being turned off deliberately, which is a different and better outcome than dying slowly from neglect.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a project genuinely still needs to stay running, versus being deliberately turned off

contentSections.title: Neglect and a deliberate decision produce different outcomes for the same project

contentSections.body: A side project from over a year ago is still technically live: a small hosting bill still charges monthly, a domain still renews, and nobody — including its own developer — has visited it in months. Nothing about this is a crisis, and that's exactly the problem: it's not urgent enough to ever force a decision, so it just quietly continues, costing a small amount of money and attention, indefinitely, by default.

contentSections.scenario: A small side project, genuinely useful to nobody currently (no real users, no personal use), still costs a small recurring amount — hosting, a domain renewal — and still exists as one more thing on a running mental list of "things I should probably check on."
contentSections.question: What's the actual difference between this project quietly continuing by default, versus its developer deliberately deciding to turn it off?

options.label: A deliberate decision to turn it off is a real choice, made once, that ends the ongoing cost and the ongoing mental overhead — continuing by default is neither, it's just the absence of a decision
There's no real difference — either way, the project ends up in roughly the same state
Continuing by default is actually better, since it preserves the option to revisit it later

feedback.deliberate-better: Right. Turning something off deliberately is an actual, completed decision — the small recurring cost stops, the mental overhead of "I should check on that sometime" stops, and if it's genuinely wanted again later, redeploying from the (still-existing) repository is a real, available option. Continuing by default isn't neutral — it's an ongoing, unexamined cost that nobody actually chose.
feedback.no-diff: The financial and attentional cost is real and ongoing in one case, and stopped in the other — "same state" ignores that one of these keeps charging a card and occupying mental space indefinitely, and the other doesn't.
feedback.default-better: The option to revisit isn't actually lost by turning something off — the code still exists in its repository, and redeploying it later (per the deploy module) is a real, available path if it's genuinely wanted again. "Keeping it live just in case" preserves nothing that turning it off (with the code kept) would actually lose.

contentSections.concept: A project that's no longer genuinely used isn't neutral by continuing to run — it carries a real, small, ongoing cost (money, attention) that a deliberate decision to turn it off actually ends. The code isn't lost by turning the live version off; it stays in its repository, available to redeploy later if it's ever genuinely wanted again. Turning something off is a real, completed decision; letting it quietly continue by default is the absence of one.

contentSections.body: A genuinely useful, low-pressure question to ask periodically about any running side project: if this stopped working right now, would anyone — including me — actually notice or care within a week? If the honest answer is no, that's real, useful information, not a failure — it's a signal that turning it off (hosting cancelled, domain left to lapse if it's not worth the renewal, code kept safely in its repository) is a legitimate, deliberate choice worth actually making, rather than continuing by default.

A project nobody would notice going down isn't neutral by staying live — it's an ongoing, unexamined cost. Turning it off deliberately, with the code kept safely, is a real, completed decision, better than continuing by default.

contentSections.title: Turning something off properly, not just walking away

contentSections.body: Deciding to turn a project off is the first half — actually doing it in a way that doesn't leave loose ends (an active database still holding real user data, a domain quietly renewing for years after anyone last checked) is the second half, and it's easy to skip.

contentSections.scenario: A project is being deliberately shut down: no more real users, the decision is made. Several cleanup steps are under consideration.
contentSections.question: Select every step that's actually part of shutting a project down properly, not just stopping active development on it.

items.label: Cancel or downgrade the hosting plan so it stops billing
If any real user data exists, handle it responsibly — export or delete it, and tell any real remaining users what's happening, per the data-responsibility standard from the accounts module
Make a deliberate choice about the domain — keep renewing it if it's cheap and meaningful, or let it lapse if it isn't, rather than defaulting to either
Delete the code repository entirely, since the project is no longer active

explanation.cancel-hosting: This is the actual mechanism that stops the ongoing cost — deciding to shut down without cancelling hosting leaves the exact same recurring bill running, just alongside a decision nobody's acted on yet.
explanation.handle-user-data: If the project ever had real user accounts, the data-responsibility obligations from the accounts module don't disappear just because the project is shutting down — handling that data responsibly, and telling any real remaining users, is still owed.
explanation.let-domain-lapse-decide: A domain is a real, ongoing decision (from the deploy module) — shutting a project down is a natural point to actually decide, rather than letting the renewal continue on autopilot for years after anyone cares.
explanation.delete-repo: Keeping the code, even for a project no longer live, costs essentially nothing and preserves the option to revive it later or reference it — deleting it removes that option for no real benefit, and isn't a necessary part of shutting the live version down.

contentSections.synthesis: Shutting a project down deliberately means actually stopping the ongoing costs (hosting, and a real decision about the domain) and honoring any remaining obligations (real user data), while keeping the one thing — the code itself — that costs nothing to keep and everything to lose if it's deleted for no reason.

contentSections.body: Shutting a project down properly means actually stopping the ongoing costs and honoring any remaining data obligations — and keeping the code itself, which costs nothing to keep and forecloses every future option if deleted.

title: Practice — Triage Seven Production Incidents
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a described production incident, triage it using this module's ideas — monitoring, logging, dependency risk, and re-orientation.

learningObjectives.text: Triage a described production incident using this module's core distinctions

contentSections.title: Seven incidents, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: what monitoring would have caught, what a useful log line would have said, whether an update was routine or risky, and what a proper re-orientation or shutdown actually looks like.
The same real question every time: what specifically, from this module, would have caught this sooner or made it easier to diagnose?

title: Lab — Set Up Monitoring and a Maintenance Routine
description: Add real uptime monitoring to a deployed project, and write the monthly maintenance routine that would actually keep it running well after you've stopped thinking about it day to day.

learningObjectives.text: Set up working uptime monitoring that would actually notify you of a real outage
Produce a concrete, actionable monthly maintenance routine for a real project

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Take a real, deployed project and give it the two things this module argues every live project genuinely needs: monitoring that would actually notify you if it broke, and a written routine specific enough that following it monthly would actually catch the things this module covered.

contentSections.title: Set up monitoring and a maintenance routine
contentSections.brief: Add real, working uptime monitoring to a live project, and write a monthly maintenance routine specific enough to actually follow — not a vague aspiration, a concrete checklist covering monitoring review, dependency updates, and log review.
