contentSections.deliverable: Monitoring that would notify you, plus a written monthly maintenance routine.

stages.title: Set up uptime monitoring
stages.instructions: Using a service with a real free tier (UptimeRobot or similar), set up a monitor for a real, live project's URL. Configure a real alert (email or another channel you'd actually see) and confirm it, and test that it actually works — briefly break something (or use the service's test-alert feature) to see the alert arrive.
stages.checkpoint: You've personally received a real test alert, not just configured a monitor and assumed it works.

stages.title: Add or improve one piece of logging
stages.instructions: Find one place in the project where an error is currently logged with little or no specific context (or add a new one for a genuinely risky operation), and rewrite it to include the specific detail lesson two described — what was happening, for what specific case, and what went wrong.
stages.checkpoint: At least one log line now includes enough specific detail to actually diagnose the problem without having been there.

stages.title: Run a real dependency check
stages.instructions: Run the project's audit command (npm audit or equivalent). If anything genuinely high-severity turns up, address it. Otherwise, note what a routine update pass would look like for this project's current dependencies.
stages.checkpoint: The audit has actually been run, and any real, high-severity finding has been addressed or explicitly documented as a known, accepted risk.

stages.title: Write the monthly maintenance routine
stages.instructions: Write a concrete, numbered checklist someone could actually follow once a month: check the monitoring dashboard, run the audit command, skim recent errors, confirm the project still builds from a fresh clone. Specific enough that following it doesn't require remembering anything from this module.
stages.checkpoint: The routine is a real, followable checklist — specific steps and what to check for, not a vague reminder to 'stay on top of maintenance.'

rubric.criterion: Monitoring genuinely works
rubric.meets: A real test alert has actually been received, not just a monitor configured and assumed correct.

rubric.criterion: At least one log line is genuinely diagnostic
rubric.meets: The log line states what was happening, for what specific case, and what exactly went wrong — not a generic 'error occurred.'

rubric.criterion: A real dependency audit has been run
rubric.meets: The audit command has actually been run against the real project, with any high-severity finding addressed or explicitly documented.

rubric.criterion: The maintenance routine is concrete and followable
rubric.meets: A specific, numbered checklist someone unfamiliar with this module could actually follow, covering monitoring, dependencies, and logs.

contentSections.body: Monitoring and a written routine are what turn 'I hope it's still working' into an actual, checkable fact — the whole point of this module, made concrete for one real project.

title: Checkpoint — After Launch
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Users and Accounts, two reaching back into Deploying. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — After Launch

questions.prompt: Why is relying on a user report as the primary way to detect an outage a real, structural problem?

options.label: It has no guaranteed upper bound — a broken site with quiet users could stay broken for a long time, undetected
It's only slower than automated monitoring, not structurally different
It's actually more reliable than automated monitoring, since real users notice real problems

questions.explanation: A user report depends entirely on someone noticing and choosing to say something — many users simply leave without reporting anything, which means detection time has no real ceiling at all.

questions.prompt: What's actually missing from a log line that just says console.log("error")?

options.label: Any specific detail — what was happening, for what case, and what exactly went wrong
Nothing — it's sufficient once an alert has already flagged the problem
Only that it used console.log instead of console.error

questions.explanation: A generic error line confirms that something failed but offers no diagnostic starting point — a useful line states what was happening, for which specific case, and what exactly went wrong.

questions.prompt: Which kind of dependency update, by semver convention, is explicitly allowed to break a project's existing usage?

options.label: A major version update
A patch update
All three (major, minor, patch) carry identical risk

questions.explanation: Semver's convention explicitly reserves the right to break existing usage for major version bumps — patch and minor updates are meant to be backward-compatible.

questions.prompt: Why does a project nobody would notice going down still carry a real cost by staying live?

options.label: It continues an ongoing, unexamined cost in money and attention — turning it off is a real, completed decision that actually ends that cost
It doesn't — a project with no active users costs nothing either way
The only cost is a hypothetical security risk, nothing concrete

questions.explanation: A live-but-unused project keeps costing real, if small, money and mental overhead — a deliberate decision to turn it off (with the code kept) actually ends that, while continuing by default is the absence of a decision, not a neutral one.

questions.prompt: From Users and Accounts: why must a password be hashed rather than encrypted for storage?

options.label: Hashing is irreversible, so a breach can't recover anyone's actual password — encryption is reversible by design, the wrong property here
Encryption is simply an older technique
There's no real difference for password storage

questions.explanation: Encryption is reversible by anyone with the key — exactly the wrong property for a password. Hashing is irreversible, letting login be verified without the original ever being recoverable.

questions.prompt: From Users and Accounts: why does a server need a session mechanism to keep someone logged in?

options.label: HTTP is stateless — each request is handled independently, with no memory of an earlier login
The server remembers logins automatically as long as it keeps running
Sessions only matter on a slow connection

questions.explanation: HTTP has no memory between requests by default — a session token bridges that gap.

questions.prompt: From Users and Accounts: for a small project with real users and no dedicated security specialist, what's usually the sounder authentication choice?

options.label: An existing, established auth service
Building hashing and sessions fully from scratch, for full control
It doesn't meaningfully matter which is chosen

questions.explanation: An established auth service has absorbed far more real-world scrutiny than a small team's own from-scratch implementation typically will.

questions.prompt: From Users and Accounts: does data-responsibility (protecting data, a deletion path, honesty about collection) genuinely apply to a small, informal hobby project?

options.label: Yes — it scales down to something simpler at small scale, not down to nothing
No — these obligations only apply once a project has many real users
Only if the project charges money

questions.explanation: The underlying obligations don't disappear at small scale — they're met more simply (a manual deletion process, an informal note) rather than not at all.

questions.prompt: From Deploying: a deploy log shows success, but the live page is blank. What's the most likely cause?

options.label: The host is configured to serve the wrong output directory
The build must have actually failed despite the success message
This is always a browser caching issue

questions.explanation: A build succeeding and being served correctly are separate facts — a blank page after a clean build almost always means a misconfigured output directory.

questions.prompt: From Deploying: what does a custom domain actually cost, ongoing?

options.label: A yearly rental, roughly $10-15/year for a typical .com, separate from hosting cost
A one-time fee, owned outright after the first payment
Always bundled free with hosting

questions.explanation: A domain is rented per year from a registrar — a real, ongoing cost, and one that can be lost if a renewal is missed, which is exactly the kind of ongoing cost this module's shutdown lesson revisits.

contentSections.body: Everything in this module is about the months after launch that most tutorials skip entirely — including, honestly, deciding a project's life is over, which is a real and legitimate ending, not a failure.

title: Choosing a project you can actually finish
description: The best capstone idea isn't the most impressive one — it's the specific, honest one that's actually finishable given real, current capacity, because an unfinished ambitious project teaches and proves far less than a finished modest one.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a capstone project idea against realistic capacity, not aspirational capacity

contentSections.title: Finished and modest beats ambitious and abandoned

contentSections.body: Two capstone ideas, from two different learners at the same point in this track: one plans a multi-user social platform with real-time chat, payments, and a recommendation engine. The other plans a personal expense tracker with three screens. Six weeks later, the second project is live, tested, and documented. The first is 40% built, in a private repo nobody's seen, and increasingly demoralizing to open.

contentSections.scenario: Two capstone projects at the six-week mark: an ambitious, unfinished multi-feature platform (40% complete, nothing usable end to end yet), and a modest, finished expense tracker (100% complete, live, tested, documented).
contentSections.question: Which one actually demonstrates more, to an employer, a collaborator, or the learner's own confidence?

options.label: The finished modest project — a complete, working, deployed thing proves the entire skill set this track built; an unfinished ambitious one proves intent, not ability
The ambitious unfinished project — the scope and difficulty attempted matter more than whether it's actually done
Neither is meaningfully better — completion doesn't matter as much as the ideas involved

feedback.modest-finished: Right. A finished, modest project is real, checkable evidence: it deployed successfully, it's been tested, someone can actually click through it. An unfinished ambitious project, whatever its scope, can't demonstrate any of that — there's no live URL, no proof the whole pipeline (build, deploy, test) actually works end to end, just a private repo and an intention.
feedback.ambitious-unfinished: Ambition attempted, without a working result, is very hard to actually evaluate — a reviewer (or the learner themselves) can't tell the difference between "this would have worked" and "this had a fundamental problem that only would have surfaced at 80% done." A finished result removes that ambiguity entirely.
feedback.neither: Completion is exactly the thing this whole capstone module is testing — everything from lessons 1-4 (deploy, backend, accounts, maintenance) only actually gets demonstrated by something that's genuinely finished and live, not by an idea, however good.

contentSections.concept: A capstone's entire value is in being a finished, real, checkable thing — deployed, tested, documented — that proves the whole track's skills were actually absorbed, not just understood in the abstract. An unfinished project, no matter how ambitious or interesting its scope, can't prove any of that, because "finished" is exactly the property being demonstrated. Choosing a project genuinely small enough to finish, given real, current capacity, isn't a compromise — it's the actual point of the exercise.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the whole track's energy-aware design: real capacity varies, and a capstone chosen against an aspirational, best-possible-week version of yourself is a capstone that's likely to become the ambitious-and-abandoned example above. Choosing against a realistic, averaged sense of actual available time and energy — the same honest assessment this track has asked for from the very first module — is what makes "finished" a genuinely reachable target instead of a hope.
A finished, modest project proves everything this track built. An unfinished ambitious one, whatever its scope, proves nothing checkable — choose against real capacity, not an aspirational best week.

contentSections.title: A quick, honest filter for an idea

contentSections.body: Before committing real weeks to an idea, a short, specific gut-check catches most of the ideas that would otherwise become the abandoned example — worth running deliberately, not just trusting instinct.

contentSections.question: Put these filter questions in the order that actually eliminates a bad-fit idea fastest, before committing real time to it:
steps: Can I describe, in one sentence, exactly what this does and for whom?
Could a genuinely smaller version of this still be worth finishing, if I ran out of time?
Does this need anything (a paid API, specialized hardware, a dataset I don't have) I don't already have real, confirmed access to?
Have I built anything even roughly similar before, or is every single part of this new to me at once?
contentSections.explanation: A vague one-sentence description is often the first sign an idea isn't actually well-formed yet, so it comes first. Whether a smaller version is still worth finishing determines whether cutting scope later (lesson two) is even possible, or whether the idea only works at full size — a real risk factor to know about early. Confirmed access to anything the project genuinely depends on prevents a stall discovered mid-build. And knowing whether every part is simultaneously new is a real, honest risk signal — not a reason to avoid a stretch project entirely, but a reason to budget considerably more time and expect more detours than an idea built mostly from familiar pieces.

contentSections.body: None of these questions have a single correct answer that disqualifies an idea outright — they're meant to surface real risk honestly, before it's discovered three weeks in. An idea that fails one of these isn't automatically wrong; it's an idea that needs a specific adjustment (a smaller version, confirmed access secured first, extra time budgeted) before being committed to.

A short, honest filter — one-sentence description, a viable smaller version, confirmed access to what it depends on, how much is genuinely new — surfaces real risk before it's discovered three weeks into building.

title: Cutting scope until it fits your real capacity
description: Cutting scope isn't giving up on an idea — it's separating what the idea actually needs to be real and useful from everything that's just nice, and building only the first part first.

learningObjectives.text: Cut a project idea's scope down to a core that's genuinely finishable, without losing what makes it worth building

contentSections.title: Most of a feature list is optional. A small core usually isn't.

contentSections.body: A recipe-saving app's initial feature list: user accounts, saving recipes, tagging and search, meal planning, a shopping list generator, social sharing, and a mobile-friendly layout. Written out like this, it reads like a real product roadmap — and building all of it, for one person, in the time available, is exactly the ambitious-and-abandoned pattern from lesson one.

contentSections.problem: Cut the recipe-saving app's feature list down to a core that's genuinely finishable, without losing what makes the idea actually worth building.

steps.label: Name the one thing the project is actually for
steps.work: "Save a recipe, and find it again later." Not "a complete meal-planning platform" — the single core action.
steps.why: Everything else on the list either supports this one action or is a separate, additional feature layered on top of it — naming the core first is what makes the cut possible instead of arbitrary.

steps.label: Sort every feature by whether it's required for that one core action
steps.work: Required: saving a recipe, viewing saved recipes. Not required for the core action, but adds real value: tagging/search, a mobile layout. Separate feature entirely, not a variation of the core: meal planning, shopping lists, social sharing.
steps.why: This sort is what turns a flat list of seven equally-weighted features into a clear priority order — required first, valuable-but-optional second, separate-feature-entirely last (and first to cut).

steps.label: Build only the required tier first, completely
steps.work: Accounts, saving, viewing — built, deployed, and genuinely working end to end — before touching anything from the second or third tier.
steps.why: A completely working core is a real, demonstrable project on its own, at any point lesson one's timeline runs out — exactly the property an unfinished, everything-at-once build doesn't have.

steps.label: Add from the second tier only if time genuinely remains
steps.work: Tagging and search, then a better mobile layout, added one at a time, each one leaving the project in a genuinely working state before starting the next.
steps.why: This is what lesson three's staged building is for — each addition is a real, separate stage that could be the stopping point without leaving anything broken.

faded.problem: Cut a different idea — a habit tracker with accounts, daily check-ins, streak tracking, reminders, data export, and a public profile page — down to a finishable core.

blanks.prompt: What's the one-sentence core action this project is actually for?
blanks.answer: Check in on a habit, and see your history of doing so
blanks.why: This is the single action the entire idea exists to support — everything else is either supporting it or a separate addition.

blanks.prompt: Which features are required for that core action?
blanks.answer: Accounts and daily check-ins (streak tracking is arguably part of 'seeing your history')
blanks.why: Without accounts and check-ins, there's no core action to perform at all — these aren't optional additions, they're the idea itself.

blanks.prompt: Which features are separate additions, not variations of the core, and should be cut first if time is tight?
blanks.answer: Reminders, data export, and a public profile page
blanks.why: Each of these is a genuinely separate feature layered on top of a working core, not something the core action depends on — reasonable additions later, but not part of a first, finishable version.

contentSections.procedure: Name the one-sentence core action, sort every feature by whether it's required for that action versus valuable-but-optional versus a separate feature entirely, build the required tier completely first, and add from the next tier only if real time remains — each addition leaving the project working before the next one starts.

contentSections.body: Naming the one-sentence core action first is what turns a flat, equally-weighted feature list into a real priority order — build the required tier completely before touching anything else.

contentSections.title: Cutting a feature is not the same as cutting the idea

contentSections.body: A common, understandable fear about cutting scope: that a smaller version isn't really "the idea" anymore, that it's a lesser, compromised thing. In practice, a well-cut core almost always still is the idea — just without the parts that were never actually required for it to be real and useful.

contentSections.scenario: The recipe app's core (save a recipe, find it again) is built and working. Several proposed "is this still the same idea" concerns are raised.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that's actually true about a well-cut core version of a bigger idea.

items.label: A person could genuinely use the core version for its actual purpose (saving and finding recipes), even without the cut features
The cut features aren't gone — they're just not built yet, and the same idea can be extended later if there's ever more time
Without every originally-listed feature, it's not really the same idea anymore — it's a different, lesser project
A working core, even a small one, is genuine, checkable proof of the same skills the full version would have demonstrated

explanation.still-useful: This is the actual test of whether a cut was sound: does the remaining core genuinely do the thing the idea was for? If yes — as it is here, saving and finding a recipe — the cut removed extras, not the idea itself.
explanation.cut-features-recoverable: Cutting scope for a first version is not the same as abandoning the cut features forever — a genuinely working core is a real foundation a later version can build on, whenever more time exists.
explanation.not-real-idea: The idea was never 'every feature on the original list' — it was the one-sentence core action from earlier in the lesson. A version that does that core action well is genuinely the idea, just without extras that were never required for it.
explanation.core-proves-skill: Deploying, testing, and documenting a small, real, working thing exercises exactly the same skills a bigger version would have — completion, not feature count, is what this capstone module is actually testing.

contentSections.synthesis: The fear that cutting scope produces a lesser, fake version of the idea usually doesn't hold up once the idea is correctly understood as its one-sentence core action, not its full feature wishlist. A well-cut core is genuinely the idea, genuinely useful, and genuinely extensible later — which is a strictly better outcome than an ambitious, unfinished version of the same idea.

contentSections.body: A well-cut core is still genuinely the idea — a smaller, working, useful version of it, not a lesser fake one — and it can always be extended later, which an unfinished full version never gets the chance to be.

title: Building in stages that each work
description: Building everything at once, with nothing working until the very end, means the project is broken for the entire build and there's no real stopping point if energy or time runs short — building in stages that each independently work fixes both problems at once.

learningObjectives.text: Break a project into stages that each leave the project in a genuinely working state

contentSections.title: A project that's broken until the last commit is a bad bet for variable capacity

contentSections.body: One way to build the recipe app: write all the front-end code, then all the back-end code, then wire them together, then deploy — with nothing actually working, end to end, until the very last step. If a bad week hits at any point before that last step, there's nothing to show, nothing that runs, nothing to deploy even in a reduced form.

contentSections.scenario: Two build orders for the same recipe app: (A) all front-end first, then all back-end, then wiring, then deploy — nothing works until the final step. (B) a minimal but complete vertical slice first — one working page, saving to a real (even if tiny) backend, deployed — then each following stage adds one more real piece, always leaving the deployed version working.
contentSections.question: Given this whole track's energy-aware design and variable-capacity reality, which build order is the sounder bet?

options.label: (B) — every stage leaves something real, deployed, and working, so a bad week that interrupts the build still leaves a genuinely finished, if smaller, project
(A) — it's more efficient to write all of one kind of code before switching to another
Both are equally sound — the total amount of work is the same either way

feedback.vertical-slice: Right. Building a small, complete slice first — one real feature working end to end, deployed — and adding to it one piece at a time means the project is in a genuinely finished, demonstrable state after every single stage, not just at the very end. A bad week, an interruption, a change in available time — none of these leave the project in a broken, half-built state, because it was never all-or-nothing to begin with.
feedback.horizontal: Writing all front-end code, then all back-end code, might feel more organized in the moment, but it means there's no point before the very last step where anything actually runs end to end — exactly the fragile, all-or-nothing structure this whole track's energy-aware design is built to avoid.
feedback.equal: The total work is roughly comparable, but the *risk profile* is completely different — one order has a real, working, deployable project after every stage; the other has nothing usable until the literal final step, no matter how much of the total work is already done.

contentSections.mechanism: Building a small, complete vertical slice first — touching every layer (front end, back end, deploy) for one real feature, however minimal — means the project is genuinely working and demonstrable at every stage afterward, not just at a hoped-for finish line. Each new stage adds one more real, working piece on top of an already-working foundation, rather than assembling separate unfinished pieces that only become real when everything is finally wired together at the end.

contentSections.body: This is the same lab-staging pattern from every module's lab throughout this whole track, applied to the capstone itself: 3-5 independently checkable stages, each resumable, each leaving something real behind — not a coincidence, but the deliberate through-line of the whole 100-hour architecture, now handed to you to apply on your own project instead of a pre-written lab brief.

Building a small, complete vertical slice first — and adding to it one working piece at a time — means the project is genuinely finished and demonstrable after every stage, not just at a hoped-for final step.

contentSections.title: Writing your own stages, for your own project

contentSections.body: Turning "build it in stages" from an idea into an actual plan means writing down the specific stages for your specific project, before starting — the same way every lab in this track handed you pre-written stages, except now you're the one writing them.

contentSections.intro: Write the stage plan for a project (use the recipe app, or substitute your own capstone idea) — three to five stages, each one leaving something real and working.

fields.prompt: What should the very first stage be?

options.label: A minimal but complete vertical slice: one real feature, working end to end, deployed
All of the front-end UI, fully polished, with no backend yet
The full database schema, designed for every planned feature

feedback.vertical slice, deployed: Right — a small, complete, deployed slice means the very first stage already produces something real and demonstrable, setting the pattern the rest of the stages follow.
feedback.polished front-end only: A polished UI with nothing behind it isn't demonstrable as a working project yet — it's real progress, but it doesn't leave the project in a genuinely working, deployed state, which is the actual goal of a first stage.
feedback.full schema up front: Designing for every planned feature up front tends to over-build for features that might get cut in lesson two's scoping — a schema sized for the required tier, extended later if needed, fits the staged approach better.

fields.prompt: What should mark each stage as genuinely done, before starting the next one?

options.label: The deployed version actually works, end to end, for that stage's added piece — checked by using it, not just by the code compiling
All the code for that stage is written, whether or not it's been tested or deployed yet
A rough time estimate for the stage has passed

feedback.verified working when deployed: Right — this is what actually delivers the property this lesson is about: a genuinely working, deployed project after every stage, not just written code that hasn't been proven to work yet.
feedback.code written: Written but unverified, undeployed code doesn't give a bad week anything real to show — the whole point of staging is a genuinely working checkpoint, not just progress on paper.
feedback.time elapsed: Time passing has nothing to do with whether the stage actually produced a working result — a stage is done when it's verified working, regardless of how long it took.

contentSections.synthesis: A real stage plan names a small, complete, deployed starting slice, and defines "done" for every later stage as genuinely verified working — not written, not estimated, actually working when used. This is what turns "build it in stages" from a nice idea into a plan that actually protects the project against a bad week landing mid-build.

contentSections.body: A real stage plan starts with a small, complete, deployed slice, and defines every later stage's 'done' as verified working, not just written — that's what actually protects the project against an interrupted build.

title: Finishing: the last 10% nobody warns you about
description: The core feature working is usually the fun, motivating 90% — error states, a real README, basic polish, and actually testing the thing as a stranger would is the unglamorous last 10%, and it's the part most abandoned projects actually died at.

learningObjectives.text: Identify and complete the specific, unglamorous tasks that turn a working feature into a genuinely finished project

contentSections.title: The feature works. The project isn't done.

contentSections.body: The recipe app's core feature — save a recipe, find it again — works, end to end, deployed. It feels finished. It isn't: what happens if someone submits a recipe with an empty title? Is there a README a stranger could follow to run it locally? Has anyone actually tried using it who wasn't the person who built it?

contentSections.scenario: A project's core feature works correctly for the exact inputs and sequence of actions its own developer has personally tried. Nothing has been tested with unexpected input (an empty field, a very long one), there's no README, and nobody except the developer has ever used it.
contentSections.question: Is this project actually finished?

options.label: Not yet — a project only its own developer has ever successfully used, with no handling for unexpected input and no way for anyone else to run it, has real, common gaps left
Yes — the core feature working for its intended use is the actual definition of done
It depends entirely on how impressive the core feature is

feedback.not-finished: Right. "Works for exactly the input and sequence its own developer already tried" is a real, common, and specific gap — a stranger's first real use of almost any project surfaces an input or action nobody anticipated, and without a README, nobody but the original developer can even attempt to run it in the first place. Neither of these is a minor nice-to-have; both are part of what 'finished' actually means for something meant to be shown to someone else.
feedback.finished: The core feature working under ideal, developer-tested conditions is real, necessary progress — but it's specifically the part that's easiest to build and easiest to feel done about, precisely because it's the part that got tested constantly, by hand, throughout development. The parts that get skipped are exactly the ones this lesson is about.
feedback.depends: Impressiveness of the core feature and whether the project is actually finished are separate questions — even a genuinely impressive core feature, untested against unexpected input and undocumented for a stranger, has the same real gaps as a modest one.

contentSections.concept: "Finished" includes a specific, unglamorous set of tasks that tend to get skipped because the core feature working already feels like the finish line: handling unexpected or invalid input gracefully rather than breaking or showing a raw error, a README that lets a genuine stranger actually run the project from a fresh clone, and having someone other than the original developer actually try to use it. None of these are exciting to build, and all of them are part of what separates a demo from a genuinely finished, shippable project.

contentSections.body: This last 10% is disproportionately often where abandoned side projects actually stall — not because the hard, interesting part (the core feature) didn't get built, but because the unglamorous remainder felt like it could wait, and "later" never quite arrived. Budgeting real, specific time for it — not leftover time, actual planned time — is what gets a project from working demo to genuinely finished.

The core feature working is the exciting 90% and the easiest to feel done about, precisely because it's the part that got tested constantly during development — the unglamorous last 10% (error handling, a real README, a stranger's first use) is where most abandoned projects actually stall.

contentSections.title: Watching a stranger use it is the fastest way to find what's actually missing

contentSections.body: A developer's own use of their own project is the least reliable test of whether it's genuinely finished — they already know exactly what to type, in what order, and never trip over anything, because they built the thing that's being tested.

contentSections.question: Put these into the order that would actually find the most real, missing gaps before calling a project finished:
steps: Try the project yourself, but deliberately with unexpected input — an empty field, a very long one, clicking things out of the intended order
Write (or update) the README as if for a genuine stranger, then follow it yourself from a fresh clone to check it's actually accurate
Ask someone else — even someone non-technical — to try using the deployed project with no guidance from you
Fix whatever broke or confused someone in the previous step, then ask again if there's time
contentSections.explanation: Deliberately unexpected input, tried by the developer themselves, catches a real category of bug quickly and cheaply, before involving anyone else. Testing the README by actually following it fresh catches documentation gaps the developer wouldn't otherwise notice, since they never need the README themselves. A genuine stranger's unguided first use is what surfaces things a developer, however deliberately trying to break their own project, still can't fully replicate — a stranger doesn't know what's supposed to happen next, which is exactly the perspective that finds real gaps. Fixing and re-testing closes the loop, the same proof-of-meaningfulness idea from the testing module, applied to "does this project actually work for someone else."

contentSections.body: This doesn't need to be elaborate — a five-minute favor from a friend, watching over their shoulder (or a screen share) as they try the deployed project with zero guidance from you, reliably surfaces things weeks of solo testing never would, because they'll do the one thing you structurally can't: use it without already knowing how it works.

A developer testing their own project, however carefully, can't fully replicate a stranger's perspective — a five-minute unguided test from someone else reliably finds real gaps that weeks of solo testing won't.

title: Writing about what you built
description: A finished project nobody can find, understand, or verify is worth a fraction of one that's clearly written up — a good build account is specific, honest about tradeoffs, and lets a stranger actually understand what happened without talking to you.

learningObjectives.text: Write a build account of a real project that a stranger could actually learn from

contentSections.title: "I built an app" tells a reader almost nothing

contentSections.body: Two ways to describe the same finished recipe app: "I built a full-stack recipe app with React and Node," versus a paragraph that says what the app actually does, what was hard about it, one real decision that was made and why, and what would be different with more time. The first sentence is technically true and forgettable. The second is the actual, specific story of the project.

contentSections.scenario: A build account reads: "I built a full-stack recipe app using React, Node, and PostgreSQL. It has user authentication and a responsive design." Every word is accurate.
contentSections.question: Why does this kind of write-up, despite being accurate, tell a reader so little about the actual project?

options.label: It's a list of technologies and features, not an account of what was actually built, what was hard, or any real decision that was made along the way
It's too short — the real problem is length, not content
It's inaccurate about the technologies used

feedback.tech-list: Right. Naming the tech stack and feature list is real information, but it's the same shape every project's write-up could have — it says nothing specific about this particular project: what it actually does for someone, what was genuinely difficult, what tradeoff got made and why. A reader learns what was used, not what happened.
feedback.too-short: Length isn't the actual problem — a much longer version of the same tech-and-feature list would still tell a reader almost nothing specific about this particular project's real story, just with more words doing the same job.
feedback.inaccurate: Accuracy isn't the issue here at all — every claim in the example is true. The problem is that true, generic statements about technology used are a different kind of information from an actual, specific account of what was built and why.

contentSections.mechanism: A tech-and-feature list answers "what was used," which is the least interesting question about a finished project to almost everyone reading it — a hiring manager, a collaborator, future-you. What actually differentiates one project's write-up from a thousand similar ones is the specific story: what it does for a real person, what turned out to be genuinely hard and why, one real decision and its actual tradeoff, and an honest note on what's missing or would change with more time. That specificity is what makes a build account worth reading at all.

contentSections.body: A genuinely useful structure, short enough to actually write: what it does, in one or two sentences, for a real person in a real situation (not "a recipe app," but "lets someone save a recipe from any site with one click and find it again by ingredient"); the one thing that was genuinely hard, and how it got solved (or didn't, and what the workaround was); one real tradeoff — a scope cut from lesson two, an architecture decision — and the honest reason behind it; and what's explicitly missing or would be different with more time, stated plainly rather than hidden.

A tech-and-feature list answers the least interesting question about a project — what it does for a real person, what was genuinely hard, one real tradeoff, and what's honestly still missing is the actual, specific story worth writing.

contentSections.title: Honesty about limits is a strength here, not a confession

contentSections.body: A specific instinct worth resisting while writing this: smoothing over every rough edge, cut corner, and unfinished piece, as if admitting them makes the project look worse. In practice, it does close to the opposite.

contentSections.scenario: A build account is being drafted for the recipe app, which — honestly — has no automated tests beyond the deploy module's earlier work, a scope deliberately cut per lesson two, and one specific feature (tagging) that was started and abandoned when time ran short.
contentSections.question: Select every honest statement worth including, rather than smoothing over.

items.label: Naming the specific features that were deliberately cut, and why
Mentioning the tagging feature that was started and abandoned, and what would need to happen to finish it
Stating honestly what level of testing actually exists, rather than implying more than there is
Replacing all of the above with a vague, uniformly positive summary that avoids specifics entirely

explanation.cut-scope: Naming a deliberate cut, with the actual reasoning (from lesson two), demonstrates real judgment — the ability to scope something to what's actually finishable is a genuine, valuable skill, and hiding the cut hides the evidence of that skill.
explanation.abandoned-feature: An honestly labeled abandoned feature, with a real note on what finishing it would take, reads as self-aware and realistic — very different from either hiding it or leaving it to be discovered, unexplained, by someone poking around the code.
explanation.test-coverage: Overstating test coverage is the kind of claim that's easy to check and embarrassing to have been wrong about — an honest, specific statement of what actually exists is more credible, not less, than a vague implication of more.
explanation.vague-positive: A uniformly positive, non-specific summary is exactly the tech-and-feature-list problem from the first pod, applied to limitations instead of features — it protects nothing, since specificity (including honest specificity about gaps) is what made the write-up worth reading in the first place.

contentSections.synthesis: Specific honesty about what's incomplete or imperfect doesn't undercut a build account — it's part of what makes the whole thing credible and specific rather than generic and promotional. A reader (a hiring manager, a collaborator) reads honest limitations as self-awareness and real judgment, which is a genuinely valuable signal a purely positive summary can't provide.

contentSections.body: Naming a real cut, an abandoned feature, or genuinely thin test coverage isn't a confession — it's specific, credible evidence of the judgment this whole capstone module has been asking for, and it reads as self-awareness, not weakness.

title: Practice — Cut Seven Over-Scoped Project Ideas Down to Shippable
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given an over-scoped project idea, cut it down to a genuinely finishable core using this module's ideas — the one-sentence core action, required-versus-optional, and staged building.

learningObjectives.text: Cut an over-scoped project idea down to a genuinely finishable core

contentSections.title: Seven ideas, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: naming the one-sentence core action, sorting required from optional, planning stages that each work, and being honest about what a real write-up should say.
The same real question every time: what's the smallest version of this that would still genuinely be the idea, and could actually get finished?

title: Lab — Ship Your Capstone Project
description: Take a real idea of your own from a one-sentence core action to a deployed, tested, documented project with a real build account — the full arc of this entire module, and in many ways this entire track, applied for real.

learningObjectives.text: Take a project idea from scoping through staged building to a genuinely finished, deployed, documented result
Write an honest, specific build account of the finished project

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's whole arc, for real: choose something you can actually finish, cut it to its real core, build it in stages that each work, push through the unglamorous last stretch, and write about it honestly. Everything from every earlier module in this phase — deploying, a backend if it needs one, accounts if it needs them, monitoring — is fair game to actually use here.

contentSections.title: Ship your capstone project
contentSections.brief: Take an idea of your own — reasonably scoped from the start, per lessons one and two — from nothing to a deployed, tested, documented project with a real build account. This is the biggest single deliverable in the phase, staged specifically so a bad day at any point doesn't cost the whole thing.
contentSections.deliverable: A deployed project with tests, a README, version history and a written build account.

stages.title: Choose and scope the idea
stages.instructions: Pick a project idea and run it through lesson one's filter and lesson two's scoping. Write down the one-sentence core action, and the required-tier feature list — nothing else, for now.
stages.checkpoint: A one-sentence core action and a short, required-only feature list exist in writing.

stages.title: Build and deploy the first vertical slice
stages.instructions: Build the smallest complete version of the core action — touching whatever layers it genuinely needs (front end, and a backend and/or accounts only if the idea actually requires them, per the earlier modules in this phase) — and deploy it to a real, live URL.
stages.checkpoint: A live URL exists, and the one core action genuinely works end to end when you try it yourself.

stages.title: Add remaining required-tier pieces, in stages
stages.instructions: Add anything else from the required-tier list, one piece at a time, each one committed, deployed, and verified working before starting the next — the staged-building discipline from lesson three, applied for real.
stages.checkpoint: The full required-tier feature set works, deployed, with each addition individually verified along the way.

stages.title: Do the unglamorous finishing work
stages.instructions: Handle at least one real unexpected-input case gracefully, write or update a real README a stranger could actually follow, and — if at all possible — get one other person to try the deployed project with no guidance and note what actually confused or broke for them.
stages.checkpoint: At least one input edge case is handled, the README has been personally verified by following it fresh, and ideally a real stranger's first use has surfaced at least one real gap.

stages.title: Write the build account
stages.instructions: Write the honest, specific account from lesson five: what it does for a real person, what was genuinely hard, one real tradeoff and why, and what's honestly still missing.
stages.checkpoint: The build account is specific and honest, not a generic tech-and-feature list.

rubric.criterion: The project is genuinely deployed and working
rubric.meets: A real, live URL exists, and the core action works end to end when actually tried, not just in theory.

rubric.criterion: Scope was deliberately cut, not accidentally incomplete
rubric.meets: A written one-sentence core action and required-tier list show a real, deliberate scoping decision, not an abandoned larger plan.

rubric.criterion: Building genuinely happened in stages
rubric.meets: Commit history or notes show each addition was verified working before the next one started, not one giant final commit.

rubric.criterion: The unglamorous finishing work is real
rubric.meets: At least one edge case is handled, the README is personally verified to work from a fresh clone, and version history exists.

rubric.criterion: The build account is specific and honest
rubric.meets: It states what the project does for a real person, one genuine difficulty, one real tradeoff, and what's honestly still missing — not a generic summary.

contentSections.body: This is the whole track's argument, made physical: a small, honestly-scoped, genuinely finished thing is worth more than an ambitious, unfinished one — and you now have the receipts to prove you can build one.

title: Checkpoint — Capstone — Build and Ship Something Real
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from After Launch, two reaching back into Checking Your Own Work. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Capstone — Build and Ship Something Real

questions.prompt: Between an ambitious, 40%-built, unfinished project and a modest, fully finished one, which actually demonstrates more?

options.label: The modest finished one — it's real, checkable evidence the whole pipeline (build, deploy, test) actually works
The ambitious unfinished one — scope attempted matters more than completion
Neither — completion doesn't matter much either way

questions.explanation: A finished project is checkable, real evidence; an unfinished one, however ambitious, can't demonstrate that the whole pipeline actually works end to end.

questions.prompt: What's the actual first step in cutting an over-scoped idea down to a finishable core?

options.label: Naming the one-sentence core action the whole idea is actually for
Removing exactly half of the originally listed features
Designing the full database schema for every planned feature first

questions.explanation: Naming the core action first is what turns a flat, equally-weighted feature list into a real priority order — required, optional, and separate-feature-entirely.

questions.prompt: Why build a project as a small, complete vertical slice first, rather than all front-end then all back-end?

options.label: It leaves the project genuinely working and demonstrable after every stage, not just at a hoped-for final step
It's simply faster in total build time
It avoids the need for a backend entirely

questions.explanation: A vertical slice, deployed early, means a bad week or interruption never leaves the project all-or-nothing broken — something real exists after every stage.

questions.prompt: Why does a project's core feature working feel like the finish line, even when real work remains?

options.label: It's the part that got tested constantly, by hand, throughout development — unexpected input, documentation, and a stranger's use haven't been tested at all
Because nothing else genuinely matters once the core feature works
It doesn't — most projects correctly stop as soon as the core feature works

questions.explanation: The core feature is disproportionately well-tested by its own developer during building — the unglamorous remainder (edge cases, docs, a stranger's use) is a real, separate, often-skipped category of work.

questions.prompt: From After Launch: why is relying on a user report the wrong primary way to detect an outage?

options.label: It has no guaranteed upper bound — many users simply leave without reporting anything
It's only slightly slower than automated monitoring
It's actually the most reliable method available

questions.explanation: A user report depends entirely on someone noticing and choosing to say something, with no real ceiling on how long that could take.

questions.prompt: From After Launch: what's missing from a log line that just says "error occurred"?

options.label: Any specific detail — what was happening, for what case, and what exactly went wrong
Nothing, once an alert has already flagged the failure
Only that it should have used a different logging function

questions.explanation: A useful log line states what was happening, for which specific case, and what exactly went wrong — a generic line offers no real diagnostic starting point.

questions.prompt: From After Launch: which dependency update, by semver convention, is explicitly allowed to break a project's existing usage?

options.label: A major version update
A patch update
All three carry identical risk

questions.explanation: Semver's convention reserves the right to break existing usage for major version bumps specifically.

questions.prompt: From After Launch: is a project nobody would notice going down neutral to leave running?

options.label: No — it's an ongoing, unexamined cost; a deliberate decision to turn it off actually ends that cost
Yes — an unused project costs nothing either way
Only if it's costing money, not if it's free

questions.explanation: A live-but-unused project keeps costing real money and attention — turning it off deliberately is a real, completed decision, not the same as continuing by default.

questions.from: Three modules back — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: what's the concrete way to prove a test would actually catch a real bug?

options.label: Temporarily break the code it tests and confirm the test fails, then revert and confirm it passes again
Give the test a longer, more detailed name
Run the same test twice in a row

questions.explanation: Watching a test go red on deliberately broken code, then green again on the real code, is the actual proof it checks something meaningful — the same standard this module's lab applies to a stranger's unguided first use.

questions.from: Three modules back — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: why is testing edge cases more valuable than re-testing the ordinary middle case repeatedly?

options.label: The ordinary case is already exercised naturally by a developer's own manual use — edges are where untested assumptions usually break
Edge cases are simply faster to write tests for
There's no real difference in value

questions.explanation: A developer naturally exercises the ordinary case constantly while building — it's the edges, and a genuine stranger's unguided use, where real, untested gaps actually show up.
